What Talent Needs to Know 7 opportunities · 6 challenges
Opportunities
  • The companies that make anime collect about $3.2 billion of a $28 billion business, and the route to a larger share is equity in the title itself, which carries the overseas revenue a production fee never touches. (Rights Ownership)
  • Whether a court accepts that a working market for licensing a face, voice or script already exists decides whether AI training is something talent gets paid for or something talent cannot stop. (Rights Ownership)
  • If rentals hold at week eight, an early home release mainly moves money out of the theatrical gross, which is the number most backend and box office bonuses are paid on. (Project Economics)
  • Patreon is paying for a writer's name, likeness and weekly output with a revenue guarantee, which puts a price on an audience the writer built on someone else's platform. (Rights Ownership)
  • The three creators kept the property, so a buyer who wants Eavesdropping as a traditional series licenses it from them, with 282 million views already on the record. (Rights Ownership)
  • Voice actors locked in their pay through 2030, and the AI terms, still unpublished, decide how their recordings can be reused or replicated across those four years.
  • The money on Instagram's long-form tab is an upfront payment for non-exclusive posts, so a creator collects it and keeps the same show on YouTube, where the ad revenue share already exists. (New Revenue Stream)
Challenges & Headwinds
  • A filmmaker who gets a Netflix theatrical run still gets a run that two of the three national chains can decline, and a two-week window ahead of streaming gave them little reason to clear screens for it.
  • Flawless's consent-based approach lived in its studio relationships, and the tools have gone to a buyer without those relationships, so the protection that travels with a dubbed performance is the AI language in the actor's own contract.
  • Star Wars and Marvel actors recorded these lines, so what they earn from a soundboard on an AI app depends on whether their contracts count it as merchandising or as promotion.
  • Every production company and creator brand runs a Meta business account, so if these terms take effect, keeping work out of Meta's products could come down to closing the account.
  • Witherspoon owns Hello Sunshine again after Candle likely lost hundreds of millions on it, and she is running it at half the headcount around film, TV and the book club.
  • A buyer that has now told investors its video business is profitable will price new deals to protect that line, so talent with proven franchises, sports-adjacent formats or a box office record has the leverage at Amazon, and everyone else should expect harder questions on cost.
Anime Production Houses Now Take Equity in Their Shows to Share in $16 Billion of Overseas Sales
Overseas sales reached $16.1 billion of Japan's $28.18 billion anime business in 2025, but only $3.2 billion flowed back to the companies that make the shows.
Japan's anime industry grew 15.8% to $28.18 billion in 2025, according to the Association of Japanese Animations (AJA), presented at TIFFCOM. Overseas revenue rose 17% to $16.1 billion, about 57% of the total; domestic revenue rose just over 14% to $12 billion. Revenue reaching production companies, as distinct from the production committees (the investor groups that finance and own most anime), rose 8% to $3.2 billion. AJA's Masahiro Hasegawa said more production companies now take an equity position in their works to keep the IP and share in overseas revenue.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The companies that make anime collect about $3.2 billion of a $28 billion business, and the route to a larger share is equity in the title itself, which carries the overseas revenue a production fee never touches.
The Facts
  • Japan anime industry 2025: $28.18 billion (JPY4.45 trillion), up 15.8% (AJA Anime Industry Report, presented at TIFFCOM).
  • Overseas revenue: $16.1 billion (JPY2.54 trillion), about 57% of the total, up 17%. Domestic: $12 billion (JPY1.9 trillion), 43%, up just over 14%.
  • 2024 comparison: overseas sales grew 26% while domestic was mostly flat. Overseas first overtook domestic in 2020.
  • Revenue flowing back to anime production companies (not production committees): $3.2 billion (JPY505 billion) in 2025 vs $2.95 billion (JPY466 billion) in 2024, up 8%.
  • Masahiro Hasegawa, editor-in-chief of AJA's Anime Industry Report: more production companies are taking an equity position in their works, holding on to IP and participating in overseas revenue.
  • Demon Slayer: Kimetsu No Yaiba The Movie, Infinity Castle grossed about $800 million worldwide in 2025, the highest-grossing Japanese film of all time. Chiikawa The Movie has grossed about $159 million worldwide in 2026.
  • Japan's IP360 initiative targets $127 billion (JPY20 trillion) in content exports by 2033, including $38 billion (JPY6 trillion) for anime.

CAA and Hollywood Stars Told the OpenAI Court a Licensing Market for Their Work Already Exists
The Human Consent Foundation, CAA and voice-actor and music groups filed a 31-page brief in The New York Times case against OpenAI and Microsoft, signed by stars including Scarlett Johansson, Robert De Niro and Julia Roberts.
The Human Consent Foundation, a nonprofit Cate Blanchett co-founded, filed an amicus brief (an outside party's argument to the court) on Friday in the Southern District of New York, joined by CAA, the Music Artists Coalition, the National Association of Voice Actors, Writer, Inc and the Creative Coalition on AI. It answers OpenAI and Microsoft's claim that licensing training data is cost-prohibitive and impossible to value: "The creative industries already have in place a proven infrastructure and workflows to clear rights for dispersed works at scale." OpenAI points to briefs backing fair use, including one from the U.S. government.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Whether a court accepts that a working market for licensing a face, voice or script already exists decides whether AI training is something talent gets paid for or something talent cannot stop.
The Facts
  • Filed: late Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, Southern District of New York, in The New York Times v. OpenAI and Microsoft (suit filed December 2023; the Times moved for summary judgment last month).
  • Filers: Human Consent Foundation (founded as RSL Media in May by Nikki Hexum and Cate Blanchett; registry launched in June; backed by Steven Soderbergh), joined by CAA, Music Artists Coalition, National Association of Voice Actors, Writer, Inc, Creative Coalition on AI.
  • Appendix signatories include Anne Hathaway, Emma Thompson, Dan Levy, Ron Howard, Madonna, Olivia Wilde, Ariana DeBose, Bette Midler, Christine Vachon, Helen Mirren, Dave Eggers, Greg Berlanti, Julia Roberts, Paul Feig, Ram Bergman, Rian Johnson, Robert De Niro, Rosario Dawson, Scarlett Johansson, Vince Gilligan and the Stan Lee Foundation.
  • Brief: "Defendants have argued that licensing creative works for AI training is cost-prohibitive... The creative industries already have in place a proven infrastructure and workflows to clear rights for dispersed works at scale and cost-effectively."
  • Blanchett: "If someone wants to use my face, my voice or my image, they ask me first. There is a contract. There is a conversation."
  • Hexum: "There is already a functioning market and infrastructure for licensing creative work."
  • OpenAI cited a Friday blog post listing briefs in support of fair use, including from the U.S. government (as of last month). Microsoft did not respond.
  • Day earlier: SAG-AFTRA, WGA and AFM brief said fair use "would render moot the terms the unions and the industry agreed to at the bargaining table" (filed 10/29).

Marcus Says an Early Home Release Wins Few Extra Rentals and Costs Box Office
Greg Marcus cited industry data that the same customers rent a film whether it reaches homes in week two or week eight, and asked studios to stop home-release ads during theatrical runs.
Marcus Corp. chairman and CEO Greg Marcus said on the company's third-quarter call and to Deadline that the propensity to buy a $20 to $25 premium home rental is about the same from week two through week eight. His argument: studios lose few rentals by waiting and gain theatrical box office. He also asked studios to hold "available at home" marketing until a film's exclusive run ends. Universal has promised a 45-day exclusive window for major releases from 2027, and Skydance has committed to 45-day and 90-day windows with limits on home-viewing marketing.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): If rentals hold at week eight, an early home release mainly moves money out of the theatrical gross, which is the number most backend and box office bonuses are paid on.
The Facts
  • Greg Marcus, chairman and CEO, Marcus Corp., on the Q3 call: "The propensity to buy transactional video on demand at that price really is about the same in week 2 through week 8."
  • PVOD/TVOD generally follows theatrical at about 45 days; Marcus put the rental price at $20 to $25 for a couple of days. Consensus window to SVOD is about 90 days; Marcus wants it longer.
  • Marcus: "available at home" emails during the run send "a message you should wait" and are "very, very deleterious."
  • Windows by studio (Deadline): Disney's are the longest; Universal promised a 45-day exclusive theatrical window for all major releases starting in 2027; Skydance committed to 45-day PVOD and 90-day SVOD windows with restrictions on marketing home viewing.
  • Marcus Corp. reported a record third quarter, which Marcus credited in large part to younger audiences returning to cinemas. He said he wants more dramas and comedies to bring older audiences back.

Regal and Cinemark Passed on Netflix's Imax Run for the Fincher and Pitt Cliff Booth Movie
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth now plays its two-week Thanksgiving Imax window almost only at AMC, about 200 U.S. screens of 550 worldwide, before Netflix streams it Dec. 23.
Netflix planned its first Imax exhibition for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, directed by David Fincher from Quentin Tarantino's script with Brad Pitt returning as Cliff Booth: a two-week Imax-exclusive run at Thanksgiving, then Netflix on Dec. 23. Regal and Cinemark will not play it, TheWrap reports, so the run becomes close to AMC-exclusive at about 550 screens worldwide, 200 of them in the U.S. An insider said Netflix expected the two chains to give those screens to the second week of Lionsgate's Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, projected to open to at least $65 million.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A filmmaker who gets a Netflix theatrical run still gets a run that two of the three national chains can decline, and a two-week window ahead of streaming gave them little reason to clear screens for it.
The Facts
  • Film: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth; director David Fincher, writer Quentin Tarantino; stars Brad Pitt, Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Peter Weller.
  • Plan: Netflix's first-ever Imax exhibition, a two-week Imax-exclusive Thanksgiving run, Netflix premiere Dec. 23.
  • Regal and Cinemark will not play it during the corridor. Result: about 550 Imax screens worldwide, about 200 in the U.S., nearly all AMC; also a few smaller venues (the New Beverly; the Vista in December, on 35mm).
  • Competition: Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (Lionsgate), second week at Thanksgiving; presales ahead of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes; projected opening at least $65 million. Ballad opened to $44 million in 2023, added $42 million over the five-day Thanksgiving weekend, finished $347.6 million worldwide.
  • AMC context: screened the Stranger Things finale at 231 locations last New Year's Eve; took part in La Bola Negra, the first film for which Netflix reported box office.
  • Precedent: Glass Onion's two-week Thanksgiving 2022 run in mainstream theaters; Netflix did not share grosses.
  • Sourcing: "TheWrap has learned"; an unnamed insider on Netflix's expectations; first reported by Puck.

Flawless's AI Dubbing Tools, Built on Actor Consent, Were Sold in a UK Insolvency
Administrator BTG sold the TrueSync dubbing and DeepEditor tools to TBellScout, a startup owned by Elastic founder Steven Schuurman, after Flawless Holdings filed for administration this month.
Flawless raised $100 million from wealthy individuals to build AI dubbing tools endorsed by SAG-AFTRA and used on hundreds of Hollywood productions, including Fall and Watch the Skies. Its UK company, Flawless Holdings, filed for administration (the UK equivalent of Chapter 11, run by an outside insolvency firm) earlier in October. BTG, appointed by lender Sprk Capital, sold TrueSync and DeepEditor to TBellScout, owned by Dutch billionaire Steven Schuurman, who confirmed the deal to Deadline. Co-founders Scott Mann and Nick Lynes still control Flawless AI Inc., the U.S. company that held the studio relationships.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Flawless's consent-based approach lived in its studio relationships, and the tools have gone to a buyer without those relationships, so the protection that travels with a dubbed performance is the AI language in the actor's own contract.
The Facts
  • Flawless spent $100 million, raised from wealthy individuals rather than venture capital, building SAG-AFTRA-endorsed AI dubbing technology.
  • Assets sold: TrueSync (visual dubbing; named one of Time's Best Inventions) and DeepEditor (AI post-production; changes dialogue and performance without reshoots). Buyer: TBellScout, owned by Steven Schuurman, founder of Elastic. Schuurman confirmed the acquisition and declined further comment.
  • Seller: Flawless Holdings Limited (UK trading company, founded 2020), which filed for administration earlier in October. Administrator BTG was appointed by Sprk Capital, a UK tech lender holding fixed and floating charges over Flawless.
  • Flawless's third tool, the rights management platform Artistic Rights Treasury, is not named among the assets sold.
  • Scott Mann and Nick Lynes remain in control of Flawless AI Inc., the U.S. business that built the studio relationships on a consent-based approach; they are said to be exploring a new venture. Amit Kapur became co-CEO in March.
  • Credits: Fall (AI used to remove swearing for a PG-13), Watch the Skies (first theatrical feature with immersive AI dubbing, released with XYZ Films), The Book of Solutions, Tatami, Smugglers, Vincent Must Die, The Light. Studios have largely declined to disclose their AI use.

Patreon Will Match a Writer's Revenue in Exchange for Their Name and Likeness
Patreon offers established Substack writers a revenue match to switch, asking in return for two posts a week, a podcast and marketing rights to their name and likeness.
The Ankler reports that subscriber growth on newsletter platforms has slowed; Taylor Lorenz said her User Mag lost a third of its paid subscribers in recent months. Platforms are competing for writers who already have audiences. According to a source familiar with Patreon's offers, Patreon matches a writer's existing revenue to cover losses from the move, in exchange for at least two posts a week, a podcast and the right to the writer's name and likeness for marketing. Patreon said it has no standard template for its deals. Beehiiv charges a flat monthly fee against Substack's 10% revenue cut.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Patreon is paying for a writer's name, likeness and weekly output with a revenue guarantee, which puts a price on an audience the writer built on someone else's platform.
The Facts
  • Patreon offer terms (one source familiar with the offers): match of the writer's existing revenue to mitigate subscriber loss after switching; minimum of two posts per week; a podcast; the right to the writer's name and likeness for marketing. Patreon: no standard template, does not comment on individual agreements.
  • Taylor Lorenz, User Mag (about 97,000 to 98,000 subscribers): lost a third of paid subscribers in the past several months; "Newsletters are cooked."
  • Substack: raised $100 million at a $1.1 billion valuation last year; went from 4 million to 5 million paid subscriptions in four months last year and has not announced a new milestone. Says the app drove nearly 800,000 paid subscriptions in six months.
  • Beehiiv: paid subscription revenue on track for $35 million this year, up 84% from 2025; charges a flat monthly fee that scales. CEO Tyler Denk says writers who leave Substack cite slower recommendations and its 10% cut.
  • Breaker Media (Lachlan Cartwright): 45,000 subscribers, profitable, expanding into events with Bilt as sponsor of three dinners.
  • Newpress (Johnny Harris and Iz Harris) raised $12 million; former 60 Minutes EP Bill Owens is joining.

Nicolas Alayo, Kaleigh Howland and Christian Sullivan created and star in Eavesdropping, a serialized romantic comedy told in episodes a few minutes long.   • Eavesdropping: scripted romantic comedy, episodes a few minutes long, on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube; currently in season 3.

  • Revenue: Patreon (15% of 9,000 subscribers pay for early access), brand-integration deals, live screenings (next at the Kult L.A., Nov. 13).
  • Creators and stars: Nicolas Alayo, Kaleigh Howland, Christian Sullivan. Alayo: "We wanted to be where the people were. We didn't want to wait for permission."

  • Howland: "The barrier for entry is close to zero for posting to social." Fans organize on Discord.

Voice Actors Ratified a 12.6% Raise and New AI Terms That Run Through 2030
SAG-AFTRA members approved the TV Animation and Basic Cable Animation agreements with 94.95% of the vote; the four-year deals run from July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2030.
SAG-AFTRA's new animation contracts with the AMPTP give voice actors a 12.6% wage increase over four years, enhanced protections around AI use, residual gains and higher health, pension and retirement contributions. The agreements take effect retroactively from July 1, 2026. SAG-AFTRA president Sean Astin called it "a dignified deal with essential AI protections." Neither the union's statement nor Deadline's report spells out the new AI terms.
Potential Talent Implication: Voice actors locked in their pay through 2030, and the AI terms, still unpublished, decide how their recordings can be reused or replicated across those four years.
The Facts
  • Vote: 94.95% in favor of the 2026 Television Animation Agreement and Basic Cable Animation Agreement with the AMPTP.
  • Term: four years, effective retroactively July 1, 2026; expires June 30, 2030.
  • Terms reported: 12.6% wage increase over the term; enhanced protections around AI use; residual gains; increases to the Health Plan and to pension and retirement plans.
  • Sean Astin, SAG-AFTRA president: "a dignified deal with essential AI protections." Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, national executive director: animation performers are "entitled to meaningful protections around AI and wages that reflect the value of their labor."
  • Negotiating committee co-chairs: Bob Bergen and David Jolliffe.

Disney Licensed Star Wars and Marvel Sound Clips to an AI Voice App
Voicemod's 5.7 million monthly users can now play quotes and sound effects from The Mandalorian & Grogu in Twitch and Discord chats, with more Star Wars and Marvel boards to follow.
Voicemod, an AI voice-modifying platform, said Friday it will add soundboards from Star Wars and Marvel projects under a deal with Disney. Users play quotes and sound effects as reactions on social and gaming platforms; Variety reports the tools do not appear to let users make their own voices sound like the characters.   • Voicemod: AI voice-modifying platform, 5.7 million monthly active users; used on Twitch, Discord and other social and gaming platforms.
  • Deal: soundboards from Star Wars and Marvel projects. First boards, from The Mandalorian & Grogu, live as of Friday, Oct. 30; more Star Wars and Marvel boards later. Financial terms were not reported.
  • Variety: the boards work as "sound memes"; users do not appear able to make their own voices sound like Din Djarin or Grogu.

Meta's New Business Terms Would Let It Scrape Business Accounts for Its Products With No Opt-Out
The Copyright Alliance called the terms "unconscionable," a court in Oslo temporarily barred them, and Meta said the Nov. 20 start could slip again pending industry consultation.
Meta's updated business terms would apply to commercial accounts on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, Threads and WhatsApp. The current draft lets Meta use scrapers and crawlers "to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products"; an earlier draft also said "train" and was revised after publisher pushback. The Copyright Alliance, whose members include the RIAA, NMPA, Universal Music Group, ASCAP and BMI, said the terms still allow broad scraping for generative AI, let Meta ignore robots.txt (the standard do-not-crawl signal), and offer no opt-out. Meta says content owners can still use robots.txt.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): Every production company and creator brand runs a Meta business account, so if these terms take effect, keeping work out of Meta's products could come down to closing the account.
The Facts
  • Terms: updated commercial terms for business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, Threads, WhatsApp; effective date moved from Oct. 30 to Nov. 20 on Oct. 23; Meta now says the consultation "could extend beyond November 20, in which case we'd delay implementation." Reuters reported an indefinite delay.
  • Earlier draft (reported by Nieman Lab Oct. 15): Meta "may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of" its products. Current draft drops "train."
  • Copyright Alliance (Oct. 27), CEO Keith Kupferschmid: the terms "could allow Meta to scrape any business user's content and use that scraped content, much of which is protected by copyright, in Meta's own business products, including for advertising, and to train and ground the company's AI products." No opt-out; accept or terminate the account.
  • Meta (Andy Stone, VP Communications, Oct. 28): "We do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders." To Reuters: "content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences."
  • Oslo court (Oct. 28) temporarily barred implementation on a challenge from ten Norwegian media groups including NRK and Schibsted, pending a final ruling.
  • Earlier complaints from publishers and advertisers to EU and UK antitrust authorities (Reuters).
  • Letters: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (Oct. 23) and Sen. Adam Schiff (Oct. 24).
  • Copyright Alliance says it represents more than two million individual creators and 15,000 organizations.

Hello Sunshine Cut Half Its Staff Weeks After Witherspoon Bought It Back
About 30 people are out, and the rest now work on film, TV, the book club and the marketing and partnerships around them, Deadline reports.
Hello Sunshine, which Reese Witherspoon and the French studio group Mediawan bought from Candle Media earlier this month, is laying off about 30 people, half its staff. A source told Deadline the cuts were expected and refocus the company on its core areas: film, TV and the book club, plus related social and digital marketing and partnerships. Candle's original deal valued Hello Sunshine at $900 million; the new price was not disclosed, and sources told Deadline that Candle, backed by Blackstone, likely lost hundreds of millions. Co-founder Seth Rodsky joined the board with Witherspoon and Mediawan representatives.
Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): Witherspoon owns Hello Sunshine again after Candle likely lost hundreds of millions on it, and she is running it at half the headcount around film, TV and the book club.
The Facts
  • Layoffs: about 30 employees, roughly 50% of staff (Deadline, source familiar; TheWrap and Variety also report 50%).
  • Remaining focus: film, TV, Reese's Book Club, related social and digital marketing, partnerships.
  • Ownership: re-acquired earlier in October 2026 from Candle Media (Blackstone-backed) by Witherspoon with Mediawan; price undisclosed.
  • Prior valuation: $900 million in the initial Candle deal. Sources: Candle likely lost hundreds of millions.
  • Mediawan also owns Brad Pitt's Plan B and The Chernin Group interests.
  • Board: Witherspoon, co-founder Seth Rodsky, Mediawan representatives.
  • Credits: Big Little Lies, The Morning Show, Where the Crawdads Sing, Little Fires Everywhere, Daisy Jones & The Six, From Scratch, The Last Thing He Told Me.
  • Hello Sunshine declined to comment.

Instagram Is Paying Creators Up to $500,000 to Post Long Videos and Has Not Promised a Revenue Share
Business Insider reports offers of $50,000 to some creators and podcasters, scaling to $500,000 in some deals, all non-exclusive, while Adam Mosseri calls existing creator payments "R.O.I. negative."
Meta is testing Features, an Instagram tab for videos up to 90 minutes. Puck's Julia Alexander writes that Instagram has no preroll or mid-roll ads and no revenue-share program like YouTube's; Instagram CEO Adam Mosseri and product VP Tessa Lyons say there are no plans to add those ad formats, and Mosseri has not committed to sharing revenue. To seed the tab, Instagram is offering creators and podcasters about $50,000, and up to $500,000 in some deals, for non-exclusive long-form posts, per Business Insider as cited by Puck and The Ankler. Creators can bring their own sponsorships and branded content.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): The money on Instagram's long-form tab is an upfront payment for non-exclusive posts, so a creator collects it and keeps the same show on YouTube, where the ad revenue share already exists.
The Facts
  • Features: Instagram tab testing videos up to 90 minutes in certain countries (announced Monday, Oct. 26).
  • Seeding payments: about $50,000 to some creators and podcasters; some deals described as up to $500,000 (Business Insider, via The Ankler and Puck). Non-exclusive.

Amazon Said Prime Video Is Now Profitable, With Revenue in the Tens of Billions
Andy Jassy told investors Prime Video is "now profitable in its own right" at a revenue run rate in the tens of billions, and Amazon MGM Studios has passed $1.2 billion in 2026 box office, in a quarter where the stock fell about 6 percent after hours on an EPS miss and a $220 billion AI capex year.
Amazon reported Q3 revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12 percent [R], and record operating income of $28.1 billion at a 13.9 percent margin [R], but EPS of $1.89 missed the $1.96 consensus [R]/[2nd] and the stock fell about 6.1 percent after hours [2nd]. Inside the call, Jassy said "Prime Video has emerged as a significant business with a revenue run rate in the tens of billions of dollars, now profitable in its own right" [call]. The release adds that Amazon MGM Studios has exceeded $1.2 billion in global box office this year on Project Hail Mary and Verity, that Thursday Night Football is averaging 17.7 million viewers in its best start ever, and that Reacher season four drew 66 million viewers in 28 days [R]. Video and music expense rose 7 percent to $5.9 billion in the quarter, against 20 percent over nine months [R]. Advertising grew 11 percent to $19.6 billion on a Prime Day timing shift, with high-teens growth guided for Q4 [R]. Capex stays at about $220 billion for 2026 and will be higher in 2027 [R]/[call], and trailing free cash flow is an outflow of $42.4 billion [R].
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A buyer that has now told investors its video business is profitable will price new deals to protect that line, so talent with proven franchises, sports-adjacent formats or a box office record has the leverage at Amazon, and everyone else should expect harder questions on cost.
The Facts
  • Q3 2026: net sales $201.9B (+12%) [R]; operating income $28.1B vs $17.4B, 13.9% margin [R]; EPS $1.89 vs ~$1.96 consensus [R]/[2nd].
  • AWS: $46.0B (+39%), operating income $17.8B, $184B run rate [R]; growth "north of 40%" guided for 2027 and 2028 [call].
  • Prime Video: revenue run rate "in the tens of billions," "now profitable" [call]; no segment P&L disclosed.
  • Amazon MGM Studios: more than $1.2B global box office in 2026 to date (Project Hail Mary, Verity) [R].
  • TNF 17.7M average viewers through six games (+16%); NBA season two opener 2M+ US viewers; Reacher S4 66M in 28 days [R].
  • Video and music expense $5.9B in Q3 (+7%), $18.8B over nine months (+20%) [R, 10-Q].
  • Advertising $19.6B (+11%), subscription services $14.0B (+11%) [R]; Q4 ad growth guided to the high teens [R].
  • 2026 cash capex ~$220B [R]; Q3 cash capex $75.9B [call]; trailing free cash flow outflow $42.4B [R].
  • AMZN about -6.1% after hours on 10/29, to $228.90 [2nd].

The Guilds Told the OpenAI Court a Fair Use Ruling Would Void Their AI Licensing Terms
SAG-AFTRA, the WGA East and West and the AFM filed a 34-page amicus brief Thursday in the New York copyright case against OpenAI, citing the AI bargaining right they won this year.
The four unions asked the federal court hearing the consolidated case brought by the New York Times, other outlets and authors including George R.R. Martin and John Grisham to reject a categorical fair use exemption (a blanket legal permission) for training AI models. The brief says the 2026 contracts gave writers and actors a notice-and-bargaining right over third-party licenses of covered work for AI training, and that a ruling that training is fair use "would render moot the terms the unions and the industry agreed to at the bargaining table." Fair use, the unions argue, must stay a case-by-case call.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The AI terms the guilds won in 2026 pay off only if training needs a license, so whether actors and writers are ever paid when their work trains a model may turn on this ruling as much as on any contract.
The Facts
  • Filers: SAG-AFTRA, the American Federation of Musicians, the Writers Guild of America East and West. Joint amicus brief, filed Thursday, October 29, 2026; 34 pages.
  • Case: consolidated copyright action in New York federal court against OpenAI. Plaintiffs include the New York Times, Florida and Arkansas papers, The Intercept, Sarah Silverman, the Authors Guild, and authors Ta-Nehisi Coates, George R.R. Martin, John Grisham, Michael Connelly, Jonathan Franzen and Jodi Picoult, among others.
  • Ask: reject a categorical fair use exemption for AI training; decide fair use case by case.
  • Brief: "The harms of unlicensed training fall not just on companies like the News Plaintiffs, but on the countless professionals behind the work."
  • Brief: a blanket exemption would allow a "potentially enormous transfer of value" from creators to corporations.
  • Contract hook: in 2026 negotiations the writers and actors guilds won a notice-and-bargaining right for third-party licenses of covered work used to train commercial generative AI systems.
  • Brief: "These negotiated provisions presuppose that training on covered work is a use that can be licensed and that the people whose work is used have a stake in the terms."

Row K Has Stopped Distributing Films a Year After Buying Four at Toronto
Owner Media Capital Technologies froze all film distribution after Row K missed October payroll and rent, laid off four staff and fell behind on settlement payments, TheWrap reported.
Row K launched in August 2025, backed by Christopher Woodrow's Media Capital Technologies, and bought four films at the Toronto festival weeks later. Only two were released. Dead Man's Wire grossed under $4 million worldwide in January after Row K spent about $5 million to acquire it and $5 million to market it, an insider told TheWrap. The company gave up Maude Apatow's Poetic License, which Sony Pictures Classics picked up. President Megan Colligan left in the spring and Row K made no further acquisitions. MCT said it will refocus on its core business.

The Facts

New York and New Jersey Count Star Salaries in Their Film Credits and California Does Not
Congress returns Nov. 9 aiming to pass the federal film credit by Dec. 18; New York's 30 percent credit counts above-the-line pay, while California's $750 million program still excludes it.
Backers of the Motion Picture, Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act expect it to pass in the lame-duck session that opens Nov. 9, before a Dec. 18 Senate adjournment target; the IRS would run it. Film commissioners and studio executives told TheWrap that other states, not California, may collect the surge. New York and New Jersey count above-the-line salaries (pay for stars, directors, writers and producers) toward their credits. California raised its cap from $330 million to $750 million but still excludes them, and one unnamed studio executive said it "wouldn't be in my top 5 states to shoot."
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): In New York and New Jersey a star's fee counts toward the credit and lowers the picture's net cost, and in California it does not, which makes the cast attachment part of the location math on any studio film shooting in the U.S.
The Facts
  • Bill: Motion Picture, Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act; built on U.S. labor costs; would stack on state incentives. President Trump endorsed the idea in early September.
  • Timing: Congress returns Nov. 9; government funding deadline Dec. 11; targeted Senate adjournment Dec. 18. Congressional insiders say the IRS would run it, with no new federal film commission.
  • Union-commissioned study: major-studio production spending located in the U.S. fell from 74% in 1999 to 42% in 2024.
  • New York: $800 million cap plus a separate $100 million indie program; above-the-line spending counts toward the 30% base credit, up to a 40% limit of other qualified costs.
  • New Jersey: 30% base including above-the-line, up to 44% with bonuses; a $250 million program for studios that lease stages in the state (Netflix, Lionsgate, Paramount at 1888 Studios in Bayonne).
  • Georgia: uncapped; output fell from 412 productions and $4.4 billion of direct spending in 2022 to 245 productions and $2.3 billion in 2025.
  • California: cap raised to $750 million; above-the-line excluded; projects must start shooting within 180 days of approval; a 2027 push to uncap is expected. Mayor Karen Bass supports uncapping.
  • David Ellison (Skydance): "Even if you got the federal rebate, California would not be as competitive with some of the other states in the United States. Jersey is at 43%. Georgia is at 38%."
  • Scott Karol (SP Media Group): "We don't need to have the best tax credit. We just need a competitive one."
  • Thomas Laub (Shadowbox Studios, Georgia) on stability: the U.K. credit has been stable for 20 years; the worry is "two, three golden years" followed by repeal.

The Luca Writer Says The Holdovers Was Built on His Black List Script and Is Suing Alexander Payne
Simon Stephenson filed a copyright suit Wednesday in California federal court, alleging Payne read his script Frisco in 2013 and again in 2019, when it was submitted to him on Netflix's behalf.
Stephenson, whose credits include Paddington 2, seeks unspecified damages and an injunction (a court order) that would bar further exploitation of The Holdovers. The suit also names co-writer David Hemingson, producer Mark Johnson and distributor Focus Features. The WGA declined the dispute in 2024 because copyright claims cannot be arbitrated there. Focus bought the film at Toronto for an estimated $30 million; it grossed about $46 million and streams on Netflix. Appeals courts have recently warned judges against early dismissal of such suits, but the Servant and Moana cases ended in defense verdicts last year.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Stephenson's case rests on two dated submissions of his script to Payne, and with appeals courts keeping more of these suits alive past early dismissal, the record of who received a spec and when is what carries a writer's claim.
The Facts
  • Plaintiff: Simon Stephenson (Luca, Paddington 2, The Electrical Life of Louis Wain). Frisco made the 2013 Black List.
  • Filed Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, California federal court. Relief sought: unspecified damages and an order barring further exploitation of the film.
  • Defendants: Alexander Payne, David Hemingson, Mark Johnson, Gran Via, Honest Scholar, Mirax, Focus Features, Universal Home Entertainment.
  • Alleged access: 2013, via Payne's producing partner Jim Burke, who said Payne "did like it but was not interested in prod or directing it"; 2019, a second submission on behalf of Netflix.
  • Cited similarities: day-card structure introduced with the misused term "Under Black"; an unexplained "medical conference" line that is central to Frisco; a protagonist dressed down for offending a member of Congress.
  • Payne has said the film draws on the 1935 French film Merlusse; the suit says the premise may come from Merlusse but the structure came from Frisco.

  • Precedent cited: Gregorini v. Shyamalan/Apple (Servant) revived on appeal; Servant and Moana idea-theft cases ended in defense verdicts last year; Shape of Water case settled after a 2020 revival.

Instagram Wants Creators' Long Videos and Is Not Asking for Exclusivity
Instagram began testing 90-minute horizontal videos with U.S. creators Monday without exclusivity; the same day Netflix, which requires podcast exclusivity, hired former Apple Podcasts executive Steve Wilson to lead podcast acquisitions.
Instagram's Features product lets podcasters, comedians and other long-form creators post horizontal videos of up to 90 minutes, linked from Reels and built for Instagram's TV app, which reaches Apple TV this month. Instagram product vp Tessa Lyons said there is no exclusivity and existing sponsor deals carry over. YouTube pays qualified creators 55 percent of ad revenue and will double its Partner Program entry bar in February. Netflix's podcast deals require exclusivity; it brought on Wilson as a consultant to run acquisitions, per THR.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): Netflix wants podcasts exclusively while Instagram takes the same 90-minute episode with the sponsors attached, which leaves exclusivity as the term a creator with a video podcast can actually charge Netflix for.
The Facts
  • Instagram Features: horizontal videos up to 90 minutes, test began Monday 10/26 with select U.S. creators; already tested in Brazil; plan to expand to "tens of thousands of creators in the U.S."
  • Early creators: Emma Grede (podcast host, Skims co-founder), Monet McMichael, Preston Rakovsky, Donald De La Haye.
  • Tessa Lyons (vp product, Instagram): working on "a few different deals" with early creators; no exclusivity requirement; existing ad and branded-content deals carry over.
  • Instagram for TV launched last year on Samsung, Fire TV and Google TV; expanding to Apple TV in the U.S. Instagram is also testing Series (episodic Reels), aimed at microdrama studios and creators, U.S. launch end of 2026 or early 2027.
  • YouTube offers qualified creators 55 percent of ad revenue (THR). From February 2027, YouTube Partner Program entry doubles to 8,000 watch hours in 365 days or 20 million Shorts views in 90 days (TheWrap).
  • YouTube had 15.8 percent of all U.S. TV usage in August, per Nielsen, more than twice Netflix (TheWrap).
  • Adam Mosseri (head of Instagram): "It's very much about TV."
  • Netflix: Steve Wilson, 15 years at Apple Podcasts, later chief strategy officer at QCODE and at Daylight Media, joins as a consultant in charge of podcast content acquisition (Bloomberg first reported). Netflix podcast deals require exclusivity; Netflix has not released podcast viewing stats.

Skydance Offers Buyouts as Talent Weighs Elon Musk's $1 Billion Stake
David Ellison and Ynon Kreitz offered Skydance staff voluntary buyouts and ordered five office days Monday; the merged company carries nearly $90 billion of debt and a $2 billion savings target.
The memo, obtained by Deadline, phases in a five-day office week across Skydance, which closed its $110 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery this month; Warner staff had been on three days. Puck's Kim Masters reports, citing unnamed executives, that Elon Musk's $1 billion investment alarmed people on the Warner lot, and one high-value creative with business there described fear. Masters expects Skydance to spend to show it is talent-friendly, within what its debt allows. Senator Ron Wyden called the investment "an unholy alliance."
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Skydance is trying to show it is still a place talent wants to work while it cuts $2 billion and services its debt, and the creatives it most wants are the ones who can set the price of that proof.
The Facts
  • Memo from co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreitz (10/26): five-day in-office policy across Skydance, phased by location (largest sites: Los Angeles, New York, Atlanta, London); Voluntary Buyout (VBO) Program with individual terms and a decision window.
  • Paramount had already returned to five days; WBD was at three.
  • Skydance closed its $110 billion acquisition of WBD earlier in October; combined debt near $90 billion (Deadline); Puck cites an $80 billion debt load and $6 billion in synergies.
  • Ellison has committed to at least $2 billion in cost savings, part from layoffs (Deadline).
  • Elon Musk invested $1 billion in Skydance; John Malone predicted SpaceX could invest up to $10 billion (Puck).
  • Puck (unnamed exec): "People are freaking out." Masters: Skydance "can, and likely will, counter by throwing piles of money around to establish its talent-friendliness."
  • Alex Gibney's documentary Musk is still set for HBO Max in early 2027 (Puck, HBO source).
  • Malone said Netflix was told by the administration it had no chance of regulatory approval for its WBD bid (Puck; Netflix declined to comment).

Japan's $5 Million Floor Is Keeping Smaller Shoots Out of Its Incentive
Tokyo Vice producer Alex Boden said Japan's IP360 incentive now requires about $5 million of local spend while most Japanese films cost $1.5 million to $3 million; Netflix asked for certainty over size.
IP360 replaced the JLOX scheme, which offered up to a 50 percent cash rebate and drew Tokyo Vice, Rental Family and Drops of God to Japan. At an MPA seminar at the Tokyo International Film Festival, Boden said the new floor excludes independent and lower-budget projects, that Shogun and Pachinko scouted Japan and shot elsewhere, and that a panel decides awards. Netflix APAC production affairs director Debra Richards said a lower incentive is fine "so long as it's certain" and called the current one opaque.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Under $5 million of local spend, a Japan-set project gets no IP360 money, and above it a panel decides case by case, which keeps the rebate out of the financing plan until it is approved.
The Facts
  • IP360, run by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI), replaced JLOX (introduced 2022, up to 50 percent cash rebate on qualifying spend). METI target: $127 billion (JPY20 trillion) in Japanese content exports by 2033.
  • Minimum spend raised to about $5 million (JPY800 million) of Japan spend; Boden: most Japanese films cost $1.5 million to $3 million.
  • Improvements Boden credited: more funds, more projects supported, a two-year application window.
  • Boden's asks: lower the floor, widen which producers may apply, automatic approval in place of a panel.
  • Debra Richards (Netflix, Director APAC Content & Studio Production Affairs): "You could have a lower incentive, that's fine, so long as it's certain and the criteria are clear."
  • Shogun and Pachinko scouted Japan and shot elsewhere. Productions that shot under JLOX (Rental Family, Drops of God, Neuromancer, Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty!) did so before the changes.
  • Event: MPA seminar 'Strengthening Japan's Production Environment' at the Tokyo International Film Festival (runs to November 4).

Netflix's True-Story Shows Are Drawing Defamation Suits That Survive Early Dismissal
On October 20 a Florida judge let two Miami officers' defamation suit over The Rip proceed, and Netflix withdrew its Baby Reindeer appeal, sending Fiona Harvey's case back to the trial court.
Judge Daryl Trawick refused to dismiss claims by officers Jason Smith and Jonathan Santana against Falco Pictures, which registration records tie to Ben Affleck and Matt Damon's Artists Equity. Separately, a Ninth Circuit en banc ruling barred interim federal appeals of anti-SLAPP (early dismissal of speech suits) denials, so Netflix dropped its Baby Reindeer appeal.

The Facts
  • The Rip: Netflix film starring and produced by Ben Affleck and Matt Damon, a fictionalized account of a 2016 Miami police raid that recovered $20 million in drug money.
  • Plaintiffs: officers Jason Smith and Jonathan Santana. Filed in federal court in May; withdrawn and refiled in Florida state court.
  • Defendant: Falco Pictures, which registration records indicate is owned and operated by Artists Equity. Netflix holds the copyright and is not a defendant.
  • Ruling (Judge Daryl Trawick, October 20): defamatory reading is a jury question; plaintiffs adequately alleged the film is "of and concerning" them; portrayal could support actual malice; depicting officers lying to obtain consent to search could be defamation per se; intentional infliction of emotional distress claim proceeds.
  • Baby Reindeer: September 2024, a federal judge in Los Angeles denied Netflix's anti-SLAPP motion against Fiona Harvey, noting the episode one title card "This is a true story." The Facts
  • Opt-out or non-compliance: production still qualifies for 96 percent of its allocated credit.

  • Participation: 105 of 115 productions opted in across the past eight application windows (commission figure).

  • UCLA: minority lead actors on streaming fell from 51 percent (2024) to 36 percent (2025).
  • Calculation: 4 percent of $17 million = $680,000.

Talent Departures Pushed Sarandos to Fire Netflix's Content and Film Chiefs
Bloomberg's Lucas Shaw reports that Dan Lin passed on projects from partners including Peter Chernin and Steven Spielberg, many of the powerful people he turned down went to Sarandos, and Bajaria and Lin were fired two days apart.
Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos fired chief content officer Bela Bajaria on October 14 and film chief Dan Lin two days later, Lucas Shaw reported in Sunday's Bloomberg Screentime, based on conversations with more than a dozen people. US engagement had slipped, measured in qualified play days (days a month a customer watches). Shaw reports talent was the deciding issue: the Duffer Brothers, Noah Baumbach and Shawn Levy left, David Fincher did not renew his deal, and partners Lin turned down went to Sarandos. Sarandos told analysts that Peter Rice "understands talent relations." Netflix declined to comment.
Potential Talent Implication: Two Netflix executives lost their jobs partly because partners Dan Lin turned down went over his head to Sarandos, and Peter Rice starts the job with a public mandate to win those filmmakers back.
The Facts
  • Sarandos told Bajaria she was fired around 4:30 p.m. on Wednesday, October 14; he dismissed Lin two days later. Peter Rice, a Disney and Fox veteran, replaced Bajaria.
  • Engagement: the average customer is spending fewer days a month watching Netflix (qualified play days) and less time on the service; the problem was most acute in the US.
  • Shows that fell short, per Shaw: Little House on the Prairie; new seasons of Beef lost most of their viewers. Netflix won its fewest Emmys in a decade.
  • Lin, brought in by Bajaria in 2024, pared the film slate and passed on ideas from partners including Peter Chernin and Steven Spielberg; "many" of the powerful people he turned down reached out to Sarandos.
  • Departures cited: the Duffer Brothers, Noah Baumbach and Shawn Levy left for other companies; David Fincher opted not to renew his deal (Shaw: he is taking a sabbatical, not leaving for a rival). The Duffers and Levy left to make theatrical films.
  • Lin's record cited by Shaw: most of his films this year rated "loved" on Netflix's internal MVS satisfaction metric; an Oscar contender three years running (Emilia Perez, Train Dreams, La Bola Negra).
  • Sarandos on the analyst call: "Peter Rice understands talent relations. In a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life."
  • Greg Peters at a staff town hall: "Two things can be true. We have an enviable, growing and profitable business. And, at the same time, we know there's more work to do to drive more growth."
  • Netflix is on pace for about $15 billion in profit this year; shares fell 6.6% last week, which Shaw attributes mainly to the year-end forecast.
  • Sarandos first approached Rice about managing the Warner Bros. assets during Netflix's bid for Warner Bros.; those talks picked up again in recent weeks.

Studios Are Selling Their Outtakes to AI Labs, Down to 16 Takes From Eight Cameras
Versos AI CEO Chris Keevill said at MIPCOM that his company turns studio rough cuts and multicamera takes into AI training data, and BlackRock-backed Easttree Media said it buys profit participations for a lump sum.
At a Deadline and ACF Investment Bank roundtable at MIPCOM, Versos AI co-founder and CEO Chris Keevill said his company licenses studio video libraries to AI labs for training. Buyers increasingly want multicamera footage, he said, so Versos now goes into rough cuts and edit suites "to find the 16 takes from eight cameras on the same subject." At the same table, Marc Allen of Easttree Media, backed by funds managed by BlackRock, said Easttree buys passive profit participations (backend income streams) for an upfront payment. Easttree does not disclose which rights it holds.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): Takes an actor never approved for release are now being sold to AI labs by the studio that holds the footage, and the actor's share depends on what the contract says about training use.
The Facts
  • Keevill (Versos AI): "Our side is helping studios monetize their dormant assets for AI training; it's unlocking value in those NAS drives and cold drives and whatever's held in storage and preparing raw video into a trainable dataset. And then we expose it to all the big labs, who are hungry to get at it."
  • Keevill: "Increasingly, [the buyers] want multicam views, which is good for the studios. We're now going into the rough cuts and the edit suite to find the 16 takes from eight cameras on the same subject." Versos works with big and small libraries.
  • Allen (Easttree Media, Founding Partner): Easttree acquires passive profit participations, in whole or in part, for an upfront payment, letting rights owners unlock cash from income streams that may run for decades. "We're there to look at and price the content and we'll give you a lump sum."
  • Easttree does not discuss which IP or owners it works with.
  • Parrot Analytics (per Deadline): TV shows based on existing IP register 3.5 times the demand of shows that are not; films based on existing IP, four times.
  • ACF Investment Bank advised on the sale of The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit IP to Embracer, Paddington IP to StudioCanal and GKIDS to TOHO.
  • Animaj CEO Sixte de Vauplane on building Pocoyo past one billion monthly YouTube views before selling to broadcasters: "You shift from selling a show to selling an audience, which is far more valuable."

SAG-AFTRA's Streaming Bonus Is Paying 700 Performers $1.5 Million for 2024 Work
About 700 performers will split roughly $1.5 million from the streaming bonus fund won in 2023, about 0.4 percent of a membership above 160,000, for high-budget SVOD work released in 2024.
SAG-AFTRA told its national board this weekend that the first payout from the streaming success bonus it won in the 2023 strike will reach about 700 performers, per Deadline. A title that clears the viewership threshold pays each principal performer 100 percent of the fixed residual; the performer keeps 75 percent and 25 percent goes to a fund run by SAG-AFTRA and AMPTP trustees, with no disclosed formula for that share. Health plan eligibility still requires $28,933 a year in union earnings, and members behind on dues will be terminated at the end of October.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): The 2023 streaming bonus reached about 700 performers in its first payout, so for a working actor the value of a streaming job still sits in the fixed residual and in clearing the $28,933 health plan threshold.
The Facts
  • Roughly $1.5 million will go from the bonus distribution fund to about 700 performers for work on high-budget SVOD projects released in 2024 (SAG-AFTRA overview of the national board plenary, Monday).
  • That is about 0.4% of SAG-AFTRA's 160,000+ members; more than 100,000 members are actors and performers.
  • Bonus mechanics: a title over the viewership threshold triggers a payment to each principal performer equal to 100% of the fixed residual; the performer receives 75%, and 25% goes to a fund controlled by SAG-AFTRA and AMPTP trustees for distribution to other members. No details yet on how the 25% is distributed or whether it is included in Monday's figures.
  • Health plan: qualifying requires $28,933 in annual union-contracted income; SAG-AFTRA agreed to deep plan cuts earlier this year in exchange for a health fund infusion.
  • SAG-AFTRA returns to its regular membership policy at the end of October: members not current on dues will be terminated.
  • Sean Astin (president), in a 12-minute video: "Cable and then streaming steadily dismantled that system, and we've spent years fighting to reclaim it. What we've won back is substantial, but it's nowhere near what it was."
  • Drake Bell, Cecily Strong, Jack Haven and Heather Matarazzo have publicly described losing or nearly losing coverage; Cheyenne Jackson launched "ONE JOB AWAY" to spotlight actors close to qualifying and reports "hundreds" of submissions.

MarVista joined in 2024 under a financing agreement with Polvino's OLF Productions: a $300,000 development fund, shared approval rights and profit participation. Polvino seeks restoration of her rights and damages.

  • Defendants: Anthony Robbins (EP of Sound of Freedom), producer Kate Cohen, MarVista Entertainment and its parent Fox Entertainment.
  • Rights history: Polvino and Cohen bought the film rights from Frankl's estate in 2016; the book has sold more than 16 million copies in over 50 languages since 1946.
  • 2024 financing agreement (MarVista–OLF): $300,000 development fund, shared approval rights, profit participation.
  • Allegations: Cohen embezzled funds and diverted development assets and rights-renewal negotiations to a new company; she told MarVista and Fox that Polvino had surrendered her rights and fees as compensation for $500,000 Polvino allegedly took from another co-owned company; Robbins acquired the rights after they expired in 2024; MarVista and Fox cited that to declare OLF in breach and negotiate with Robbins; screenplay and writer agreements proceeded under a different company.
  • Relief sought: an order restoring Polvino's rights, unspecified damages, restoration of OLF to active status.
  • All claims are allegations in the complaint; THR did not report a defense response.

Elvis Presley's Catalog Owners Are Suing Anthropic for $41 Million Over 274 Songs
Authentic Brands Group and other Presley rights holders sued Anthropic on October 23, claiming Claude was trained on 274 Presley songs without permission and seeking about $150,000 per song.
Authentic Brands Group, which owns rights to Elvis Presley's music, filed a copyright suit against Anthropic on October 23 with other Presley rights holders, Pitchfork reported after viewing the filing. The suit says Anthropic trained Claude on 274 Presley songs, including "Can't Help Falling in Love," and that Claude still produces close copies. It seeks roughly $150,000 per song, about $41 million. Anthropic told Pitchfork it disagrees and will defend the case. Major labels and publishers have sued Anthropic before; Pitchfork called this one of the first such suits by the owner of a single artist's catalog.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The Presley owners are asking $150,000 a song on 274 songs, and an artist or estate that owns its catalog outright can bring that claim itself, without a label or publisher in the lead.
The Facts
  • Plaintiffs: Authentic Brands Group (Tennessee-based, per Pitchfork) and co-plaintiffs holding Presley rights.
  • Defendant: Anthropic. Filed October 23, 2026; viewed by Pitchfork.
  • Claim: Claude trained on 274 Presley songs without permission; songs named include "Can't Help Falling in Love," "Don't Be Cruel," "Farther Along," "If You Think I Don't Need You," "Run On." The suit also alleges "unlicensed derivative works."
  • Damages sought: about $150,000 per song, about $41M total.
  • Filing, quoting Claude: "These renders keep landing very close to the originals: same structure, same hooks reused with light rewording..."
  • Lead attorney Richard Busch: the defendant "has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before."
  • Anthropic to Pitchfork: "We disagree with the claims and intend to defend this case fully."
  • Pitchfork: major labels and music publishers have filed claims against Anthropic before; this is one of the first high-profile cases by the owner of a single artist's catalog.

Doug Shapiro Expects AI to Make Quality Content Abundant and Weaken Its Pricing Power
In a new essay, Shapiro argues flat consumer attention plus falling AI production costs will bring more quality content, lower hit rates, creators taking share and weaker pricing for content itself.
Doug Shapiro published part one of a two-part series on Sunday arguing that two facts are reliable enough to plan on: consumer attention is not growing, and generative AI will sharply cut creation costs. From those he predicts more quality content, more substitutable hits, lower hit rates, creators taking share and weaker pricing power for content. He expects value to move to whoever creates demand for specific content, controls the moment of consumer choice, or sells complementary products. His Morgan Stanley-based chart shows platforms such as Netflix and YouTube took almost all media value from 2018 to 2025.
Potential Talent Implication: In Shapiro's read the work itself becomes easier to replace, and what keeps its price for talent is an audience that asks for them by name plus a share of the products and services sold around the work.
The Facts
  • Title: "The Predictable Economic Consequences of Infinite Content" (part one of two; part two will cover implications for a media company). Paid post with a partial free preview.
  • Two premises Shapiro calls highly confident: "consumer attention isn't really growing and GenAI will dramatically reduce creation costs."
  • Predicted consequences: "quality content supply will explode; even high-quality content will become more substitutable; hit rates will fall; creators will take share; content pricing power will weaken; and for a lot of content, monetization will move from the content itself to complementary products and services."
  • Where value shifts: "creating differentiated demand," "coordinating demand (controlling the moment of consumer choice)," and "monetizing complements."
  • Biggest unknown, per Shapiro: who controls coordination, and whether GenAI uncouples coordination from distribution.
  • Figure 1 (source: Morgan Stanley, The Mediator): from 2018 to 2025, essentially all value created in media accrued to digital consumer platforms (Meta, Netflix, Spotify, YouTube, TikTok, Valve/Steam, Roku).

The BBC Has Found Only £200 Million of the £500 Million It Must Cut by 2028
Closing BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra in spring 2027 saves about £10 million, two insiders told Deadline; the BBC has announced about 1,200 of a planned 2,000 job cuts.
The BBC must save £500 million ($670 million) by 2028 after losing more than two million licence fee payers since 2020, and it has announced £200 million of that so far, Deadline reported Saturday. Director general Matt Brittin announced the three channel closures on Tuesday. BBC leaders also discussed merging children's channels CBBC and CBeebies and folding BBC Sounds into iPlayer. Funding talks with the government, which include a proposed "Netflix tax" (a surcharge on streaming subscriptions), leave the BBC with no view of its finances past the end of 2027.
Potential Talent Implication: The BBC has promised more spending on younger audiences without naming a figure, and until its funding settlement lands, UK producers pitching comedy and youth series are selling to a buyer that cannot see past 2027.
The Facts
  • Savings target: £500 million ($670 million) by 2028; £200 million announced to date.

Artists Equity's Indie Label Gives the Creative Team Half the Points and Sits Outside Its Netflix and Sony Deals
Amy Baer told IndieWire that AEIP films fall below the minimum budgets in Artists Equity's Netflix and Sony output deals, so they are free to sell elsewhere, and still carry streaming viewership bonuses.
Amy Baer, president of film and television at Ben Affleck and Matt Damon's Artists Equity, said its new label, Artists Equity Independent Pictures, runs on the company's model: talent takes a smaller fee up front and equity in the film. In a typical indie, she said, half the points go to the filmmaking team and half to financiers; AEIP hands the creative team its half to divide. Because AEIP budgets sit below the minimums in the Netflix streaming and Sony Pictures theatrical output deals, those deals do not bind the label, though either buyer can still acquire a film.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): An AEIP film pays less up front, but the creative team holds half the points and the film can sell to any buyer, which puts the value in how the points are split and what the film sells for.
The Facts
  • Label: Artists Equity Independent Pictures (AEIP), led by Jennifer Westin (formerly physical production at Topic Studios), reporting to Baer.
  • Model (Baer): "In a typical indie film, 50 percent of the points go to the filmmaking team, the other 50 percent go to the financiers. We just say to the creative team, 'Here's your points. Carve it up.' We're not going to tell you how to do it."
  • Output deals: Artists Equity has Netflix (streaming) and Sony Pictures (theatrical) output deals with minimum budget levels; AEIP films will typically fall beneath them and are not bound by either; Netflix or Sony can still buy one.
  • Bonuses: AEIP films still qualify for performance bonuses at streaming viewership thresholds, as on The Rip, where Artists Equity paid a percentage of salary to each of 1,200 crew members; thresholds and amounts undisclosed ("robust" views, "substantial" bonus).
  • First titles: A Woman in the Sun (writer-director Julia Cox; Renée Zellweger, Sissy Spacek, Mia Threapleton; Black Bear distributing) and Downriver (director Sam Jones; Garrett Hedlund, Jake Lacy, Jessica Biel).
  • Sourcing: packaged projects, not internal development; no low-budget slasher horror or experimental films.
  • Baer: "This is not a talent production company on steroids."

Agencies Want Producers to Get Their Shows Back From Streamers After Three Years
The American Entertainment Alliance would cap streamer exclusivity at three years for films and five years for series, and UTA's Rich Shuter told Puck that license fees would fall.
Puck laid out the terms of the American Entertainment Alliance plan to revive fin-syn (the old rules limiting network ownership of outside shows). Streamers with at least 10 million U.S. subscribers would spend half of original film and series budgets, excluding sports and library, with independent producers. Exclusive rights would end after three years for films; for series, two years after the third season airs, capped at five years after the first-season finale. The original streamer gets first negotiation on an extension but no right to match. The coalition has hired Akin Gump to lobby Congress.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The plan swaps the up-front premium for a second sale: UTA's Rich Shuter concedes streamers would pay lower license fees, and in return the producer gets the show back after three years with a library to license again.
The Facts
  • Coalition: CAA, WME, UTA, Ziffren Brittenham, Blumhouse, Imagine and Legendary among members; registered months ago at CAA's Century City address; public debut in the New York Times and on The Town.
  • Scope: streamers with at least 10 million U.S. subscribers; half of spending on original films and series, excluding sports and library acquisitions, to independent producers (companies neither owning nor affiliated with a qualifying streamer).
  • Exclusivity caps: films three years; television two years after the third season airs, outer limit five years after the first-season finale (Shuter's suggestion).
  • Extension: first negotiation right for the original streamer, no matching right.
  • Lobbying: Akin Gump retained (Lauren Rubin, Democrat; Geoff Verhoff, Republican). Pursued as separate legislation from the pending bipartisan production tax credit bill.
  • Shuter acknowledged to Puck that streamers would pay lower license fees under the plan.
  • Gardner's open questions: which agency administers it (F.C.C. or F.T.C.), who audits the 50 percent, and First Amendment exposure; cites Schurz Communications v. F.C.C. (7th Cir. 1992).

Podcasters hosting on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone can now charge monthly or annual fees for bonus episodes, ad-free listening and other perks, a direct challenge to Patreon. California's Tax Credit Now Backs 40 Percent of LA Location Shoots, and Production Is Still Falling
FilmLA counted 4,171 on-location shoot days in Los Angeles from July through September, down 4.8 percent from a year earlier, while credit-backed projects reached a record 40.3 percent of scripted location work.
FilmLA's quarterly report shows California's expanded credit, raised to $750 million a year from $330 million, now funds 62 percent of TV comedy and 49.4 percent of TV drama location days, up from about 20 percent each a year ago. Total shoot days are still 36 percent below the five-year average, per The Hollywood Reporter. Features rose 2.1 percent to 533 days; commercials, which the credit does not cover, fell 15.9 percent. Mayor Karen Bass called for an uncapped credit and a federal one. The program still does not count above-the-line costs.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Above-the-line pay still does not qualify for California's credit, so on a California show the subsidy covers crew and production costs while the talent fee is the part of the budget the producer pays in full.
The Facts
  • Q3 2026 (July to September): 4,171 on-location shoot days, down 4.8 percent year over year (Deadline); down about 11 percent from Q2 and 36 percent below the five-year average (THR). Q2 decline was 13 percent.
  • Credit share: incentivized projects 40.3 percent of scripted on-location production, nearly double a year ago.
  • TV: credit-backed projects 62 percent of TV comedy and 49.4 percent of TV drama shoot days (19 percent and 20.6 percent a year ago). THR: TV 1,400 days, down about 3 percent; drama 494 days, down 9 percent; comedy 192 days, up 143 percent.
  • Features: 533 days, up 2.1 percent; incentivized 24.4 percent, mostly independents; studio titles include 13 Going on 30 (Netflix), Cut Off (Warner Bros.), They Follow (Neon).
  • Commercials: 562 days, down 15.9 percent; not eligible for the credit; more than 41 percent below the five-year average.
  • Program: annual cap raised to $750 million from $330 million in 2025; 214 projects selected since July 2025.
  • FilmLA CEO Denise Gutches: "Overall production remains far below where Los Angeles needs it to be."
  • Mayor Karen Bass called for "an uncapped California film and television tax credit" and a federal credit.
  • ProdPro: New York production spend up 87 percent in the quarter vs. California's 17 percent.
  • THR: the open question is whether California will let above-the-line costs qualify, as most regions with credits do.
Feeds a Talent Opportunity: The Federal Credit Bill Counts Star Pay Toward 20 Percent

Senior Streaming Executives Leave Faster Than Studio Executives, a Count of 1,387 Appointments Finds
Stephen Follows counted 1,387 senior appointments since 2011: 17 percent of streaming appointees left within two years against 11 percent at studios, and 31 percent against 21 percent by year three.
Stephen Follows, a data analyst, pulled 11,802 trade stories from nine publications since January 2011 and tracked 531 senior appointments at streamers and 856 at studios. At the very top layer, a quarter of streaming chiefs left within two years against 14 percent at studios. HBO Max lost 30 percent of senior appointees within two years and Paramount+ 26 percent, while Netflix lost 15 percent and Amazon Prime Video 18 percent. Of 185 reported streaming exits, 22 percent used words of removal and 30 percent came with a restructure or a new boss.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Streaming executives leave faster than studio executives, and one in 12 reported exits mentioned a production or first-look deal, so the executive who ordered a project may be gone, or across the table as a producer, before it is delivered.
The Facts
  • 1,387 senior appointments tracked: 531 at seven streamers and 856 at traditional studios; 11,802 articles from nine publications, January 2011 to the start of October 2026.
  • Left within two years: 17 percent at streamers, 11 percent at studios; within three years 31 versus 21 percent; within five years 51 versus 36 percent.
  • Top layer (chiefs, chairs, presidents, heads of film, television, content and marketing): 247 streaming and 362 studio appointments; a quarter of streaming executives gone within two years against 14 percent at studios; half gone within four and a half years at streamers and six at studios.
  • Within two years: HBO Max 30 percent, Paramount+ 26 percent, Amazon Prime Video 18 percent, Netflix 15 percent; half of Netflix appointees were still in post after six years; at Disney half were still in post after 13 years.
  • Of 185 reported senior streaming exits: 22 percent removal words, 30 percent restructure or new boss, 26 percent another job, 4 percent leaving to start a company or produce, 2 percent retirement or personal, 16 percent no reason cited.
  • One in 12 streaming exit stories mentioned a production or first-look deal.

Netflix Is Not Pausing Margin Expansion to Spend More on Content, Guggenheim Says

Netflix reports third-quarter results on Tuesday after cutting about 6 percent of its workforce and replacing chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice. SAG-AFTRA's Microdrama Agreement Pays Leads $250 a Day on Budgets Capped at $300,000
A year after SAG-AFTRA's Verticals Agreement, dozens of microdramas are union-covered: leads get a $250 minimum for eight hours, budgets cap at $300,000, and shoots run no longer than 30 consecutive days.
TheWrap reports that SAG-AFTRA's independent Verticals Agreement, which covers vertical microdramas (short serialized video made for phones), turned one last week. The union says it has signed off on dozens of productions out of hundreds made each year. Leads receive a minimum of $250 for an eight-hour day and $468.75 for 12 hours, against a $1,246 baseline for a television day player. Producers pay pension and health contributions for every performer, union or not. Actor JT Garcia went from $600 a day on ReelShort productions to more than $1,200 a day plus 20 percent.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): The $250 lead minimum sits below what some leads are paid: JT Garcia went from $600 to more than $1,200 a day plus 20 percent, with pension and health contributions paid by the producer on top.
The Facts
  • Budget cap $300,000; most microdramas cost $150,000 to $300,000; shooting limited to 30 consecutive days.
  • Lead minimum: $250 for eight hours, $468.75 for 12 hours. Non-lead minimum: $164 for eight hours, $307.50 for 12 hours. Television day-player baseline under the 2026 television agreement: $1,246.
  • Overtime: 1.5 times after eight hours for hours nine and 10, double time from hour 11.
  • A nonmember who works one principal role on a covered vertical can use it to seek union membership.
  • Productions named: Knockout Shorts (five SAG productions), Snow Story Productions (hundreds of verticals, three union), Issa Rae's "Screentime" (TikTok and Pine Drama), Taye Diggs' "Tides of Temptation" (with Lifetime and Microhouse Films).
  • Knockout Shorts co-founder Chris Crema said leads can command rates above the minimums and his company often exceeds them in its first offer.
  • Casting director Howard Meltzer tells agents that budgets have to be $300,000 and under.
  • Jessica Johnson, SAG-AFTRA deputy chief contracts officer: producers feared the union would slow them down, "and that's just not been the case."

Screen International reports that A Woman Asleep, by artist and director Vikki Bardot, is one of 10 films in the main competition at FilmFestival Cottbus in Germany, November 3 to 8. Studios Want AI-Made Franchises but Cannot Copyright What AI Makes Alone
Arcos Labs founder Nelson Chu says several dozen studio executives want to make IP with AI, and his VN Studio logs which steps humans performed to support a copyright claim.
Under US copyright rules, purely AI-generated material generally cannot be copyrighted, which blocks studios from owning characters and franchises made that way. Nelson Chu, whose six-person startup Arcos Labs spoke with several dozen studio executives over months, says they want to stop others from generating their IP while generating their own with AI. Arcos's VN Studio, shown first to The Ankler, records which actions were done by AI and which by humans and screens for third-party IP. Chu does not guarantee a copyright, and the legal questions remain unsettled.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A studio cannot copyright what AI makes alone, so on an AI-assisted project the human work that writers, directors and artists can document could be the part that carries ownership.
The Facts
  • Source: The Ankler, Ashley Cullins, October 16, 2026, in the Dealmakers section.
  • Rule: purely AI-generated material generally cannot be copyrighted under US rules; only original works created by humans are eligible.
  • Arcos Labs: a six-person startup founded by Nelson Chu, who previously raised $50 million for the private credit startup Percent. It soft-launched this year and debuted VN in August, which it calls a fidelity recognition engine that measures how closely AI content resembles protected IP and human likenesses.
  • VN Studio: a new production platform revealed exclusively to The Ankler. It logs which actions were executed by AI and which by humans, and screens for recognizable third-party IP introduced during production. Chu will not guarantee copyright.
  • Chu: "They don't want anyone else to be able to generate their IP," describing several dozen studio executives, who added "But wait, I want to be able to generate my IP using AI."
  • A lawyer who advises studios and production companies said every studio general counsel would "fall all over themselves" for an easy tool that solves this, and that VN Studio could be "extremely pivotal" if it works as Chu describes.
  • The article notes the legal system may not give studios exclusive rights to all AI-assisted creations.

Netflix is replacing chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice, starting October 26, a day after laying off about 1,000 employees and five days before its third-quarter earnings.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos told Bajaria late Wednesday that she was being replaced, according to The Ankler. Netflix announced Thursday that Rice, a former chairman of Walt Disney Television who now produces films, will oversee scripted and unscripted series, film and live events. Puck, which broke the news, reports that film chief Dan Lin is expected to leave and that the decision belongs to Rice. The Facts
