CAA, WME and UTA Are Lobbying to Require Half of Streamer Content Budgets Go to Independent Producers
The American Entertainment Alliance, with CAA, WME, UTA, Blumhouse, Imagine and Legendary as founding members, wants a law requiring big studios and streamers to put half of original content budgets into independent projects.
The American Entertainment Alliance launched October 15 with CAA, WME and UTA among its founding members, alongside producers including Jason Blum, Peter Chernin, Ron Howard and Brian Grazer. It wants Congress to require companies such as Netflix, Disney, Amazon and Skydance to spend half of their original content budgets on independent U.S. shows and movies made by non-studio entities. The proposal resembles the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules (Fin-Syn, which restricted network ownership of programming until the 1990s repeal). The New York Times first reported the group and says the companies are likely to fight any bill.
Potential Talent Implication: Under the proposal, a producer with a show outside the studio system would be selling into a pool of buyer money reserved by law, and the Times reports top producers could see bigger paydays.
The Facts
  • The group is called the American Entertainment Alliance (AEA). TheWrap says the New York Times reported it first; Deadline carries the same news the same day.
  • Deadline lists the founding members as CAA, WME, UTA, Anonymous Content, Blumhouse, Imagine Entertainment, Jeff Sagansky, Legendary Entertainment, MRC, North Road, Producers United, Propagate Content and Ziffren Brittenham.
  • TheWrap names producers Jason Blum, Peter Chernin, Ron Howard and Brian Grazer as supporters.
  • The ask is bipartisan legislation requiring major studios and streamers to devote half of their original content budgets to independent shows and movies produced in the United States by non-studio entities.
  • Companies named as targets: Netflix, Disney, Amazon and Skydance.
  • Fin-Syn limited network ownership of programming in the 1970s and 1980s and was repealed in the 1990s; series such as Hill Street Blues, The Mary Tyler Moore Show, Seinfeld and Roseanne were independently produced.
  • CAA chief Bryan Lourd: "There are fewer people deciding what gets made and what we all see, what the consumer sees... Distribution is not the issue of the future. Who finances content is the issue."
  • UTA Vice Chair Jay Sures: "As film and television increasingly consolidate, we need a regulatory framework that puts creators first, protects industry workers and preserves competition."
  • The Times says the companies have large Washington lobbying operations and will argue they already buy plenty of programming from outside studios.

The Domestic Box Office Passed $8 Billion in 282 Days, 59 Days Ahead of 2025

Hackman Capital Partners paid nearly $2 billion for Radford in 2021, defaulted this year on more than $1 billion of related debt, and lost the lot to a Goldman Sachs-led lender takeover. The Hollywood Reporter reports Netflix is closing in on Radford at about a fifth of that price, and four of Hackman's five major L.A. properties are for sale. The Facts
  • Radford Studio Center (Studio City): Hackman Capital paid nearly $2 billion in 2021, largely debt-financed; ViacomCBS sold it to Hackman and Square Mile Capital for $1.85 billion. Hackman defaulted earlier in 2026 on more than $1 billion of debt tied to the lot; a Goldman Sachs-led lender takeover followed.
  • Netflix is "closing in on a deal at about a fifth of that price" (THR).
  • Four of Hackman's five major L.A. studio properties are being shopped, including Television City. An unnamed source: "In L.A., I think it's a curtain call for Hackman."
  • Property tax appeals since 2020 by the companies controlling the major lots: 269 appeals, about $319 million clawed back in decided cases; Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount, Universal and Sony account for more than $245 million.
  • Sony Pictures Studios (Culver City): county cut about $166.3 million, an 84 percent reduction on a $198 million assessment. WBD Burbank: argued $700 million should be as low as $212 million; county cut about $51.7 million. Universal asked in 2023 to cut its assessment from $951 million to $60 million. Paramount won about $15.6 million across 14 appeals.
  • FilmLA soundstage occupancy: 90 percent (2022), 69 percent (2023), 62 percent (2025, lowest recorded). Episodic TV was about a fifth of stage production in 2023, down from about 30 percent; scripted TV shoot days fell another 23 percent in 2024.
  • Warner Bros. lot occupancy last year: 91 percent. Simon Robinson, president of global experiences and studio operations: "We were at highs effectively for all of last year."
  • New supply: East End Studios' $230 million Mission Campus (January); Cinespace six-stage Woodland Hills facility (March); Echelon, $450 million, opening later this year; FilmLA tracks seven more planned builds or renovations.

Underlying Rights Holders, Not Skydance, Decide Whether Its Franchises Can Cross Over
J.K. Rowling, Hasbro and the Tolkien estate hold the licenses behind Harry Potter, Transformers and Lord of the Rings, and IndieWire found merger-assignment language in the licensing contracts it reviewed.
IndieWire reports that the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger does not let Skydance combine its biggest franchises, because many were licensed from outside owners. Warner Bros. would need J.K. Rowling's sign-off to put her characters in another franchise; Hasbro controls Transformers; Lord of the Rings rests on a license with the Tolkien estate. Law professors Rachel Landy and Orly Ravid said the original contracts set the limits. IndieWire reviewed licenses that reassign rights to "any entity with which [the] company is merged," so creators cannot use the change of owner to take characters back.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Rowling, Hasbro and the Tolkien estate kept approval over where their characters can appear, so a $111 billion merger still cannot put Harry Potter beside Optimus Prime; the assignment clause in a license decides who the creator works for after the next sale.
The Facts
  • Skydance closed its $111 billion merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery this week; Ellison emphasized the combined IP at the press conference on the Warner lot.
  • Rachel Landy (Cardozo School of Law): wholly original Warner Bros. material is likely 100 percent owned and transferable; much of the marquee slate is based on books, comics, toys and dolls licensed from underlying rights holders.
  • Harry Potter: Warner Bros. can keep making films and shows but would need J.K. Rowling's sign-off to put her characters in another franchise.
  • Transformers: controlled by Hasbro. Lord of the Rings: Warner Bros. adapts under "an often contentious licensing agreement" with the Tolkien estate. Star Trek: owned outright by Paramount via the 2019 CBS merger, but not the subsequent films.
  • Orly Ravid (Southwestern Law School): "Many of the underlying rights holders negotiated for lots of protections."
  • Batman is owned outright by Warner Bros. through DC Comics; Mission: Impossible is owned by Paramount via its 1968 purchase of Desilu. Insiders at both studios dismissed live-action crossovers; one executive cited animation (The LEGO Movie model) as a possible exception.

The Ankler reports the $52 billion bond sale lost buyers money within a day and that Larry Ellison's $40 billion guarantee rests on Oracle shares down more than half from their peak.   • Moody's (Sept. 29): Ba3. S&P Global (Oct. 2): net-debt-to-adjusted-earnings of about 7x in 2026 and 2027; target 3x or less by 2029.
  • Debt at close: about $80 billion. WBD started in June 2022 with about $53 billion gross debt.
  • Bond sale (The Ankler, citing Bloomberg and FT): $52 billion multi-part offering led by Bank of America and Citigroup, the largest single-day debt sale by a public company; junk portion yielded 9 percent; holders lost hundreds of millions on paper within 24 hours. Apollo, Pimco and Man Group hold a large slice.

  • Synergy target: $6 billion; efficiencies expected from tech stacks, cloud, procurement, marketing and real estate. Consent decree: at least 30 films a year for two years, 32 a year for the next three; both lots kept at least five years; cable networks negotiate carriage independently.

The Federal Film Credit Has 12 Senators and Five Weeks to Pass

Schiff, eight Southern California House Democrats and union leaders campaigned in Glendale on October 6 for the bill introduced last month: a 20 to 30 percent transferable tax credit (one a producer can sell for cash) on U.S. labor costs for film and TV.   • Timing: about five weeks in the lame-duck session after the election. Rep. Laura Friedman: "We need to have this on the president's desk by mid-December"; hopes it passes in essentially current form as part of a larger tax package.

Training AI on a Film's Own Footage Still Runs Into the Actors' Contracts
Puck's Eriq Gardner argues InterPositive's pitch of models trained only on a production's own dailies does not clear the performers' rights embedded in that footage.
Ben Affleck sold his AI company InterPositive to Netflix for a reported $600 million; it trains models on a production's own dailies and sells the results as "clean." Puck legal columnist Eriq Gardner argues a studio can own the footage without owning the right to train on the performances in it, because actors' contracts and union agreements often do not clearly authorize machine-learning training. The same question applies to cinematographers, stunt performers, choreographers and composers. He expects guild grievances, contract disputes, and chain-of-title (proof of ownership) and insurance fights over AI-assisted work.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): An actor's contract that is silent on machine-learning training leaves the performance in the dailies open to a studio's own-footage model, and every training license that gets signed adds evidence that those rights carry a price.
The Facts
  • Affleck, at Bloomberg's Screentime conference, said he used AI for "lots of things" on his Netflix film Animals and declined to give specifics; he sold InterPositive to Netflix for a reported $600 million.
  • InterPositive's pitch: outputs are "clean" because the model is trained on a film's own dailies.
  • Gardner: training a model "on our own stuff" is not the same as owning or having cleared every right the training implicates. Studios may own the footage and distribution rights, but performers' contracts and collective bargaining agreements often do not specifically authorize training "to create a new generation of synthetic performers."
  • Gardner: a public company making sweeping claims about airtight AI practices could invite a securities suit if the rights picture proves messier.
  • Gardner on licensing: the more companies license copyrighted material, the stronger the evidence that a market for training rights exists, which could make the fair-use defense harder over time.
  • Context: The New York Times v. Microsoft and OpenAI is at summary judgment; Anthropic paid $1.5 billion to settle with authors; Jeffrey Katzenberg has argued for a consent-and-credit model tied to Reactor, a generative video platform he invested in.

Germany's Production Incentive Money Ran Out in August, and Next Year's Pot Is Smaller
The DFFF and GMPF used up their €250 million for 2026 after 230 applications; waiting projects move to 2027, when the government proposes cutting the budget to €200 million.
The German Federal Film Board (FFA) told FilmFest Hamburg's Industry Days that the €250 million budget for Germany's two automatic production incentives, the German Federal Film Fund (DFFF) and the German Motion Picture Fund (GMPF), ran out in August. Applications ran 40% above the level before the rebate rose from 25% to 30% of approved German spend in 2025. Approved but unfunded projects carry into 2027, when the coalition proposes cutting the budget to €200 million, with up to €70 million reserved for features. Separately, Flanders will abolish its €3.5 million Screen Flanders fund on January 1, 2027.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Producers and directors whose financing plans count on the German rebate now face a shoot slipping to 2027 or a 30% hole in the budget, with a smaller fund waiting on the other side.
The Facts
  • Combined 2026 budget for DFFF and GMPF: €250 million, exhausted in August 2026. No new applications accepted for projects planning to start principal photography in 2026.
  • Applications through the August stop: 230, which the FFA's Jolinde Sawahn says is 40% higher than before the grant rate rose from 25% to 30% at the start of 2025.
  • Projects supported in 2026 include Netflix's The Boys From Brazil, Apple TV's Wild Things, Athos 2643, Foxfinder and Gould Lover.
  • Sawahn: "We have had more applications than funds, so we're carrying over the projects we can no longer approve this year into next year," and some projects "are now facing additional costs because they have to be postponed until 2027."
  • Proposed 2027 budget: €200 million (government austerity package). Amended guidelines due next month would reserve up to €70 million for feature films; the schemes also fund high-end series.
  • Producer Jakob D. Weydemann (Weydemann Bros): a 30% funding gap "can be a matter of survival" and might "theoretically lead to insolvency."
  • Flanders (Screen International, Geoffrey Macnab, Oct. 5): the Flemish government will discontinue Screen Flanders on January 1, 2027, removing its full €3.5 million budget. In 2025 it invested over €4 million in 22 projects, which the fund says generated €40.2 million of local spend; Belgian producers could apply for up to €400,000 as a refundable advance. Wallimage and screen.brussels continue.

Skydance Will Run All of 2027 Without Free Cash Flow
S&P, Moody's and CreditSights put Skydance at nearly $80 billion of debt and seven times earnings, with negative cash flow projected for 2027 and Larry Ellison backstopping the 2028 and 2029 leverage targets.
Skydance, the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery that formally closes October 6, starts with nearly $80 billion of debt, against about $53 billion when WBD formed in 2022. S&P Global puts leverage at seven times earnings in 2026 and 2027, with a target of three or less by 2029; if the company misses its lender targets, Larry Ellison covers the gap personally. Analysts project negative cash flow for all of 2027 and say the promised $6 billion of savings will come largely from staff cuts. Linear networks still deliver more than 70% of profit.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Skydance enters 2027 with no projected free cash flow and leverage targets Larry Ellison must cover personally if they are missed; upfront guarantees on projects there may be the hardest money to get until those targets are met.
The Facts
  • Debt: nearly $80 billion at close (Variety). Comparison: WBD had about $53 billion of gross debt as of June 2022 after assuming $43 billion from AT&T.
  • Close: formally set for October 6, 2026; the combined company is named Skydance.
  • Leverage: S&P Global and others calculate debt-to-earnings of 7 in 2026 and 2027; goal of 3 or less by 2029.
  • Backstop: if lender leverage targets for the end of 2028 and 2029 are missed, Larry Ellison makes up the difference from personal wealth.
  • Ratings: Moody's Ba3 (one notch below investment grade); S&P Global and CreditSights rate slightly higher, at investment grade.
  • Cash flow: projected negative for all of 2027 (Variety; S&P's Jawad Hussain: "2027 is not going to have any cash flow").
  • Savings: $6 billion of operational savings committed over three years, much of it from staff cuts.
  • Linear networks (CNN, TNT, TBS, Discovery, Nickelodeon, CBS): "70%-plus of the profits and almost all the free cash flow" (CreditSights' Hunter Martin).
  • Cost of the 12-state antitrust suit: probably another $500 million in higher interest on short-term debt (Martin).
  • Financing (Paramount Skydance IR, Sept. 30, 2026): priced $41.4 billion and EUR 885 million of senior secured notes and an $8.5 billion and EUR 850 million Term Loan B, including 6.30% senior secured first lien notes due 2028.
  • MoffettNathanson's Robert Fishman: "The company is going to be forced into choosing where to invest their dollars, led by streaming."

Warner Bros. Paid Tom Cruise's Full Price on an Iñárritu Original, and Digger Will Lose About $150 Million
Digger opened to $8 million domestic and $20 million worldwide on a reported $160 million net budget; Deadline's sources put the loss near $148 million on $127 million in total revenue.
Warner Bros. stands to lose around $150 million on Digger, Alejandro G. Iñárritu's satire starring Tom Cruise, Deadline reports from unnamed sources. It was the first film under the non-exclusive originals and franchise deal Warner made with Cruise in 2024. Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy greenlit it at $125 million after running it through their comps system, and an extended UK shoot took the net cost to about $160 million before a near $100 million marketing spend. Warner bought out Legendary's development costs, so Legendary is not co-financing.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Tom Cruise was carried at full price on an Iñárritu original that Deadline says belonged under $50 million, and that $150 million loss may now sit in any studio's comps when a star asks for the same price on a non-franchise film.
The Facts
  • Opening: $8 million domestic, $20 million worldwide, C+ CinemaScore; Cruise's lowest opening in 19 years. NRG tracking three weeks earlier was $17 million to $23 million.
  • Cost: greenlit at $125 million production; about $160 million net after an extended schedule at Leavesden (UK) with tax credits; near $100 million worldwide theatrical marketing. Sources tell Deadline the cost was higher.
  • Loss math (Deadline sources): about $127 million in total revenues (theatrical rentals, airline, domestic streaming, PVOD, international TV) against about $275 million in global costs, a roughly $148 million loss, assuming about $50 million global box office.
  • Deal: first project under Warner's 2024 non-exclusive originals and franchise deal with Cruise, made at David Zaslav's direction.
  • Development: Iñárritu first developed the project at Netflix with Leonardo DiCaprio eyeing it, then moved it to producer Mary Parent at Legendary, where it was developed for Cruise. Warner bought out Legendary's development costs; Legendary is not co-financing.
  • Passes: De Luca and Abdy passed on Cruise's Deeper with Doug Liman ($270 million budget ask, no script; now at Universal) and on Michael Mann's Heat 2 at $160 million (made by Amazon).
  • Quote, unnamed source involved with the Mission: Impossible films: "The problem is that there's no one in Cruise's camp to tell him 'no.'"
  • Cruise's camp argues each new release lifts the value of his $14 billion-plus library across 53 titles.
  • Comparables: The Smashing Machine ($21.1 million worldwide on $50 million) and Amsterdam ($31.2 million worldwide on $80 million).
  • Reviews: 51% on Rotten Tomatoes; RelishMix buzz fell from 8.1 to 6.4 before opening. 18 to 34 year olds were 60% of the audience.

IndieWire's Q3 horror review argues the business is measuring every release against Curry Barker's Obsession, a reported $750,000 Focus Features film that grossed more than $500 million worldwide, and notes buyers at TIFF were shopping for "the next Obsession." Evil Dead Burn grossed $72.4 million worldwide on $20 million, against $147.3 million for Evil Dead Rise on $15 million.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Buyers at TIFF were shopping for the next Obsession, but Casper Kelly's Buddy, $26.6 million on a $3 million budget from a 1,277-theater start, is the result an original horror filmmaker can actually point to in the next negotiation.
The Facts
  • Obsession (Focus Features, Curry Barker): reported $750,000 budget, more than $500 million worldwide; opened to $17.2 million in May.
  • Resident Evil (Sony, Zach Cregger): $60.2 million opening; $110.6 million in 13 days; fell 62% in weekend two; reported $75 million production budget.
  • Buddy (Roadside and Saban, Casper Kelly): $5.5 million opening in 1,277 theaters; $26.6 million domestic by end of September; never above 1,771 theaters; reported $3 million budget.

A Judge Threw Out Penske's Antitrust Case Over Google's AI Summaries of Its Articles
Judge Amit Mehta ruled that a publisher's expectation of search traffic is not an agreement; Penske, which owns Variety, Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter, can refile because the dismissal was without prejudice.
U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed Penske Media's suit against Google over AI Overviews, ruling Wednesday that antitrust law does not apply, TheWrap reports. Penske argued Google unlawfully conditions inclusion in search results on letting its articles feed AI summaries, said it lost revenue, and asked that Google be required to pay publishers to summarize articles or train AI on them. Mehta wrote that "an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works." Mehta dismissed without prejudice, so Penske may refile.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): A federal judge would not let Penske use antitrust law to make Google pay for AI summaries of its articles, and for creators whose work feeds AI tools, payment may now depend on a license negotiated up front.
The Facts
  • Ruling: U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed Penske Media Corporation's lawsuit against Google on Wednesday (Sept. 30); antitrust laws do not apply to AI Overviews of news articles.
  • Mehta: "Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an 'expectation' that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free. But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works."
  • Penske's claims (filed 2025): Google leverages search by including only publishers that permit AI-summary use; about a fifth of Google searches linking to sites show Overviews; Google should be required to pay publishers to summarize articles or use them to train AI; PMC alleged lost revenue.
  • Co-plaintiff: Chegg, alleging Google illegally scraped its content.
  • Penske owns The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline, Variety, Rolling Stone, Gold Derby, Billboard, IndieWire and Artforum.
  • Dismissal was not with prejudice; Penske may refile. PMC, Google and Chegg did not immediately comment.

Paramount and Warner Bros. Are Now One Company: Skydance
David Ellison named the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery "Skydance" on X Friday, ahead of the $110 billion merger's expected Oct. 6 close after a year of pursuit and a two-month antitrust delay.
David Ellison announced Friday that the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will be called Skydance once their $110 billion merger closes Oct. 6, following a year-long pursuit and a two-month antitrust delay from 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America. Ellison said the name avoids favoring either century-old studio: "We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one." Paramount separately priced $41.4 billion in senior secured notes and an $8.5 billion term loan B to finance the deal. Discovery Communications, public since 2008, will no longer carry its name forward.
Potential Talent Implication: Skydance opens for business carrying tens of billions in new debt, which means a highly leveraged buyer negotiating every future deal from a cost-discipline posture.
The Facts
  • Merger value: $110 billion; expected close date Oct. 6, 2026.
  • Delay: one-year pursuit by Ellison, plus a two-month hold from antitrust suits by 12 state attorneys general and the WGA, resolved via a 5-year consent decree requiring separation of Paramount/WBD operations in several business areas.
  • Financing: Paramount Skydance Corporation priced $41.4 billion and €885 million in senior secured notes offerings and an $8.5 billion and €850 million term loan B facility (announced via SEC filing Sept. 30, 2026).
  • Naming history: Skydance's August 2025 acquisition of Paramount was initially styled "Paramount, a Skydance Corporation," later "Paramount Skydance Corporation." Colloquial names "WarnaMount" and "ParaBros" had circulated in the absence of an official name.
  • Discovery Communications went public in 2008; the Discovery brand will not appear in the new corporate name.
  • Quote, Ellison: "What once was the peak, is now just the beginning... Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling."

Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy learned from news reports, not a call from David Ellison, that they will not run film at the merged company, with Paramount's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg taking over the combined unit instead.
Warner Bros. film chairs Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy will not join the merged company, Deadline and Puck reported, with Paramount's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg set to run the combined unit's roughly 30 releases a year instead.   • De Luca and Abdy have run Warner Bros.' film division since June 2022, after jumping from MGM following Amazon's acquisition of that studio; they re-upped their WBD contracts through 2030 under David Zaslav.

  • Paramount's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, current Paramount Motion Picture co-chairs, are poised to run the combined Paramount Warner Bros. film unit, per multiple sources.

  • Under De Luca/Abdy, Warner Bros. earned 30 Oscar nominations this year (tying its 2005 record) and won 11, including Best Picture for One Battle After Another.

Books Supplied 37.6% of Hollywood's Adapted Titles in 2025, the Most Since 2017

Novels accounted for 37.6% of adapted-IP film and TV premieres in 2025, the highest share since 2017, according to a TheWrap data analysis, ahead of franchise extensions (22.3%), true stories (15.2%), comics (5.1%) and video games (1.6%). The Facts
  • Share of adapted-IP premieres in 2025: books 37.6% (highest since 2017); franchise extensions 22.3%; true stories 15.2%; comics 5.1%; video games 1.6%.

2026-10-01 Thursday 11 stories

What Talent Needs to Know 6 opportunities · 5 challenges
Opportunities
  • A buyer can out-negotiate an incumbent not by topping the whole deal but by identifying which single component of it is contractually weak, the lesson in how Langley priced the one-third of Sheridan's Paramount pact (film) that actually had room to be beaten.
  • Netflix naming specific upcoming titles for wide theatrical and IMAX release, rather than treating theatrical as a one-off experiment, gives filmmakers and their reps a concrete new term to negotiate for: a guaranteed theatrical window and format, not just a backend contingent on streaming metrics. (Project Economics)
  • A filmmaker negotiating window length should treat the 90-day streaming threshold, not the 45-day PVOD threshold, as the term studios now consider load-bearing for theatrical health, since Langley singles it out as the one window "that could really undermine the cinemagoing habit." (Project Economics)
  • Any client with a large, owned audience and no business infrastructure around it is now a reachable acquisition target for the same capital that used to chase studio mergers, which argues for building the company (consumer products, live events, commercial partnerships) before a buyer prices the audience alone. (Company Building)
  • A second major platform's VFX workforce organizing in successive years, each contract carrying explicit AI guardrails from the Basic Agreement, establishes AI-use protections as a now-standard term below-the-line crews expect on any production regardless of which studio or platform is financing it.
  • A filmmaker monetizing his own AI tooling into a near-$600 million sale to the same platform distributing his film shows one concrete path for talent to capture AI's value directly, as an owned asset sold to a buyer, rather than only as a cost or threat to be negotiated around on a project-by-project basis. (Company Building)
Challenges & Headwinds
  • Every current negotiation with Paramount or Warner Bros. now touches two different decision-makers: Ellison on creative direction and talent relationships, Kreiz on the operational terms and integration that actually determine timing and budget.
  • A producer of Kennedy's stature naming the Paramount-WBD merger as a threat to the number of films getting made signals that studio-count contraction, not just deal terms at any single studio, is now a live concern shaping how indie producers plan their slates and where they shop projects.
  • Disney naming AI-driven workflow automation as part of the rationale for a third layoff round in six months signals that the cost-cutting lens reaching corporate and legal functions today is explicitly tied to the same technology now being evaluated for production and development workflows.
  • A new, private-equity-backed owner at Imagine resets who controls the company's overhead, its library monetization and its next production deal, at a moment when comparable shingles (SpringHill, Hartbeat, Hello Sunshine) have all been forced into mergers, downsizing, or unit closures.
  • Below-the-line crews and corporate staff now have two competing, named sources on the record about their own job security: the architect of the deal saying labor cuts aren't the driver, and separate reporting putting the number above 6,000, and the gap between them is itself worth tracking as the merger closes.
Paramount Confirms Kreiz as Co-CEO, Sets October 6 Close for the Warner Bros. Merger
David Ellison confirmed Mattel's outgoing CEO Ynon Kreiz as co-CEO of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery effective October 5, one day before the $111 billion merger's anticipated October 6 close.
Paramount Skydance confirmed Thursday that Ynon Kreiz, who built Barbie into a $1.4 billion hit as Mattel's CEO, will become co-CEO of the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery, reporting jointly with chairman David Ellison once the companies close their $111 billion merger on October 6. Under the division of labor Ellison announced, he retains creative direction, talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation, while Kreiz runs day-to-day operations and integration. Kreiz's five-year contract pays more than $46.5 million in year one, including a $31.5 million signing award of restricted stock, per an SEC filing.
Potential Talent Implication: Every current negotiation with Paramount or Warner Bros. now touches two different decision-makers: Ellison on creative direction and talent relationships, Kreiz on the operational terms and integration that actually determine timing and budget.
The Facts
  • Paramount Skydance confirmed Ynon Kreiz as Co-CEO of the merged company effective at closing; he starts at Paramount October 5, 2026, one day before the anticipated closing date.
  • Ellison remains Chairman and CEO of the combined company; Kreiz joins as Co-CEO and the Board of Directors. Division of labor: Ellison owns long-term strategy, creative vision/direction, talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation; Kreiz owns day-to-day management and integration of the combined businesses.
  • Kreiz spent eight years as Mattel's Chairman and CEO (since 2018); under his leadership Barbie grossed $1.4 billion worldwide and became Warner Bros.' highest-grossing film ever.
  • Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery separately announced the merger is expected to close October 6, 2026; at closing, WBD shareholders receive $31.00 per share plus $0.00277778 per day elapsed after September 30, 2026, totaling $31.01666668 per share if the close lands on October 6 exactly.
  • Per an SEC filing (Variety), Kreiz's first-year pay package at Paramount-WBD totals more than $46.5 million: $5 million base salary, a $4.9 million target bonus, a $31.5 million signing award of restricted stock units, 1.25 million shares of Class B stock as a "pre-closing award," and up to $5.1 million in RSUs granted within 15 days of closing. His 2025 total Mattel compensation was $15.1 million including a $1.6 million salary.

Kathleen Kennedy, on Leaving Lucasfilm, Warns the Paramount-WBD Merger Could Mean "Fewer Movies Get Made"
Kathleen Kennedy, who stepped down from Lucasfilm in 2026 after 14 years, told Bloomberg Screentime she feels "a bit of relief" leaving and is "worried" the Paramount-WBD merger will mean "a studio disappear[ing] and fewer movies get made."

Asked about the industry's direction, she said she is "worried" about the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger reducing the number of buyers and films made, and that she is still forming a view on AI's role in production.
Potential Talent Implication: A producer of Kennedy's stature naming the Paramount-WBD merger as a threat to the number of films getting made signals that studio-count contraction, not just deal terms at any single studio, is now a live concern shaping how indie producers plan their slates and where they shop projects.
The Facts

The ability for the studios to be able to scale the work that many of us do. I think that's the biggest worry. We'll see. If it really is 30 movies a year, we'll see."

Disney Cuts a Few Hundred More Jobs, Its Third Round Under Josh D'Amaro, With AI-Driven Automation Named as a Factor
Disney cut a couple hundred employees Tuesday, mostly in tech and HR, its third layoff round in six months under CEO Josh D'Amaro, following an internal memo that cited "automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies."
Disney initiated layoffs affecting roughly a couple hundred employees, concentrated in shared tech and HR functions, Deadline reported, a smaller cut than the two previous rounds this year: 1,000 positions in April and several hundred more in July, mostly at Pixar and National Geographic. Disney Entertainment Television and the motion picture studio are largely exempt from this round. The cuts follow a voluntary early-retirement offer to employees 50 and older with 10+ years of tenure, whose opt-in cooling-off period just ended, and a September 18 internal memo from Chief Legal and Global Affairs Officer Horacio Gutierrez warning of "hard choices" and the division becoming "a much smaller organization" through a "transformation process" that includes "automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies." D'Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston told shareholders August 5 they remain "highly focused on reducing costs across the enterprise," including "reductions in labor." Disney had 231,000 employees at the end of fiscal 2025.
Potential Talent Implication: Disney naming AI-driven workflow automation as part of the rationale for a third layoff round in six months signals that the cost-cutting lens reaching corporate and legal functions today is explicitly tied to the same technology now being evaluated for production and development workflows.
The Facts
  • Disney cut a couple hundred employees Tuesday, September 29, concentrated in tech and HR; a smaller round than the prior two this year.
  • First round: ~1,000 positions cut in April 2026, D'Amaro's first as CEO. Second round: several hundred more in July 2026, mostly at Pixar and National Geographic.
  • Disney Entertainment Television (undergoing a restructuring under new head Debra OConnell) and the motion picture studio are largely exempt from the current cuts, per Deadline's sources.
  • Disney had 231,000 employees as of the end of fiscal 2025: 172,000 in the U.S., 59,000 elsewhere; 16% part-time, 8% seasonal (largely parks and resorts).
  • The cuts follow a voluntary early-retirement offer to employees at or above director level, 50+, with 10+ years at the company; the opt-in cooling-off period ended the past weekend.
  • A September 18 memo from Chief Legal and Global Affairs Officer Horacio Gutierrez to LGA staff warned of "hard choices" about "staffing investments" and the division becoming "a much smaller organization," describing a "transformation process" including "automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies." The memo was widely shared internally.
  • In their August 5 shareholder letter, D'Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston said they are "evaluating a variety of levers, including reductions in labor and SG&A."
  • Context: between 2023 and 2025 under Bob Iger, roughly 8,000 Disney employees were let go, yielding $7.5 billion in cost savings, far above Disney's initial forecast; the current D'Amaro-era cuts are a fraction of that scale so far.

Raine Group Nears Exit From Ron Howard and Brian Grazer's Imagine Entertainment
The Raine Group is nearing a sale of its 51% stake in Imagine Entertainment, bought for $100 million in 2016, to a private equity-backed marketing firm, with Grazer personally negotiating the deal.
TheWrap reports three people close to the deal confirmed Raine has accepted a purchase price for its majority stake in Ron Howard and Brian Grazer's Imagine Entertainment, with a close expected within two weeks, though prior Imagine M&A talks have collapsed before. The sale follows Imagine's thin run of hits since the 2000s (its last global theatrical success was 2016's "Inferno") and a strained relationship between Raine and Grazer, who is negotiating the deal himself. A prior planned sale to Centricus Asset Management at a $700 million valuation fell apart in 2024 as investor interest in production companies cooled.
Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): A new, private-equity-backed owner at Imagine resets who controls the company's overhead, its library monetization and its next production deal, at a moment when comparable shingles (SpringHill, Hartbeat, Hello Sunshine) have all been forced into mergers, downsizing, or unit closures.
The Facts
  • Raine, led by co-founder Joe Ravitch and partner Erik Hodge, is exiting its 51% ownership of Imagine Entertainment, purchased for $100 million in 2016; the buyer is a private-equity-backed marketing firm whose name and the price could not be learned.
  • An Imagine representative called TheWrap's report "factually inaccurate" while declining to give further detail.
  • Imagine has been exploring a sale since at least 2024; a planned $700 million sale to Centricus Asset Management fell apart that year as interest in production companies cooled.
  • China Media Capital invested $100 million alongside Raine in 2016; FountainVest Partners invested another $100 million in 2018. By 2021 Imagine was valued around $850 million.
  • Imagine's last global theatrical hit was 2016's "Inferno"; 2025's "After the Hunt" (Julia Roberts, Andrew Garfield) grossed just $9 million worldwide, and Howard's "Eden" (Sydney Sweeney) made $2.8 million after Vertical picked it up. The last Imagine film to cross $100 million domestically was 2017's "American Made" ($135 million on a $50 million budget).
  • Comparable independent production companies have struggled: LeBron James' SpringHill Company (once valued at $750 million) merged into Fulwell 73 in 2024; Kevin Hart's Hartbeat (once valued at $650 million) has downsized repeatedly; Reese Witherspoon's Hello Sunshine shuttered its kids and family unit in 2023.
  • Howard, 72, is in post-production on the Amazon MGM Afghanistan war drama "Alone at Dawn" (Adam Driver); Grazer, 75, continues producing, including Netflix docs "Marty, Life Is Short" and "Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing." Upcoming Imagine titles: 20th Century's "Whalefall" (October theatrical), Amazon MGM's "How to Rob a Bank" (David Leitch), Netflix's "The Mosquito Bowl" (Pete Berg), and the Apple series "Wild Things" (Andrew Garfield, Jude Law). A Howard-Jim Carrey "Grinch" sequel is in early development.
  • Raine has separately been active in sports and gambling deals, including DraftKings, and most recently a $750 million catalog acquisition fund with Ares for music/artist-management company Firebird.

Donna Langley Says She Won Taylor Sheridan With a Better Film Deal, Not a Bigger One
NBCUniversal's Donna Langley says she pulled Taylor Sheridan from Paramount after a decade by upgrading the film side of his deal, since his existing Paramount film pact was only a weaker first-look arrangement.
Speaking at Bloomberg's Screentime event, NBCUniversal Entertainment chair Donna Langley said she moved on Taylor Sheridan after "disruption and instability" at Paramount, likely referring to the year-long Paramount-Warner Bros. merger process, created an opening. Her pitch centered on film rather than television: Sheridan had a film deal at Paramount, but it was only a first-look arrangement with "not as many teeth to it" as his lucrative TV pact. The film component of his new NBCUniversal deal takes effect in 2026; the TV component follows once he completes his Paramount obligations in 2028. Sheridan, who built the "Yellowstone" TV universe at Paramount, is returning to his film-writing roots with Paramount's upcoming "Call of Duty Movie" and "Sicario 3," both of which he scripted before the move.
Potential Talent Implication: A buyer can out-negotiate an incumbent not by topping the whole deal but by identifying which single component of it is contractually weak, the lesson in how Langley priced the one-third of Sheridan's Paramount pact (film) that actually had room to be beaten.
The Facts
  • Langley said her interest in Sheridan began after she "saw an opportunity" created by "disruption and instability" at Paramount; news of Sheridan's NBCUniversal deal broke in late October 2025, months before David Ellison won the bidding war for Warner Bros. Discovery.
  • Langley: "There's just a moment to kind of look around the marketplace and see if there's a competitive advantage. But really, where I started talking to Taylor was about film, because I knew that he had a film deal at Paramount, but it was a first-look deal. Didn't have as many teeth to it as his television deal."
  • The film component of Sheridan's NBCUniversal deal takes effect in 2026; the TV component follows after he fulfills contractual obligations to Paramount in 2028.
  • Sheridan broke out writing films including "Sicario," "Hell or High Water" and "Wind River" before building a TV franchise at Paramount starting with "Yellowstone" in 2018, which spawned "1923," "The Madison," "Dutton Ranch," "Lioness," "Marshals," "Landman" and "Mayor of Kingstown."
  • Sheridan wrote the scripts for Paramount's upcoming "Call of Duty Movie" and "Sicario 3," both predating his move to NBCUniversal.

Donna Langley Says Universal Is Deliberately Undoing Its Own Short-Window Training
NBCUniversal chairman Donna Langley says Universal's move to a slate-wide 45-day theatrical window is a deliberate effort to "undo the training" it gave audiences with its pandemic-era 17-day PVOD window.
At Bloomberg's Screentime event, Langley said Universal's pivot away from the 17-day premium-VOD window it pioneered with AMC in 2020 (back to a slate-wide 45-day minimum theatrical window announced earlier this year) was driven by conversations with filmmakers and a judgment that a 17-day window undermines the moviegoing habit regardless of a film's individual box office performance. Universal and other studios, including the soon-to-be-merged Paramount-Warner, are converging on a 45-day window to premium on-demand and 90 days to streaming. Langley said the streaming window, not the PVOD window, is the one that most threatens theatrical attendance, calling unlimited in-home streaming access "an all you can eat buffet."
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A filmmaker negotiating window length should treat the 90-day streaming threshold, not the 45-day PVOD threshold, as the term studios now consider load-bearing for theatrical health, since Langley singles it out as the one window "that could really undermine the cinemagoing habit."
The Facts
  • Universal struck a deal with AMC Theatres at the onset of COVID-19 allowing PVOD release as early as 17 days after theatrical, which triggered industry-wide windowing experimentation; Universal announced a slate-wide 45-day minimum theatrical window earlier in 2026, ending that era.
  • Langley: "I began to feel that it was time to try and reestablish that moviegoing habit in our audience, and just the simple math of it is that we can't really do that if we're telling them that it's available in the home in 17 days. It was really about signaling to the audience and trying to undo some of the training that we've done to tell them to kind of wait and watch it on their couch."
  • Universal had previously defended the 17-day PVOD window as reaching different audience types, including cost-conscious families; sources at Universal noted 2024's "The Wild Robot" still grossed $334 million after a 17-day PVOD release.
  • Universal and other studios, including the soon-to-close Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery, are converging on a general standard of 45 days to premium on-demand and 90 days to streaming.
  • Langley: "It's the streaming window that I think is the one to really keep an eye on, and we're all pretty consistent around that. That's the one that could, in my opinion, could really undermine the cinemagoing habit, because it's sort of an all you can eat buffet."

As Mega-Mergers Thin Out, Hollywood Dealmakers Turn to Individual Creators and IP
With fewer mega-mergers left to chase after Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery, dealmakers at Raine, Loeb & Loeb and Gerber Kawasaki say capital is shifting toward individual creators, IP, and the infrastructure that scales a one-person YouTube business into a company.
At TheWrap's TheGrill conference, Raine Group's Erik Hodge, Loeb & Loeb's John Kulback and Gerber Kawasaki's Ross Gerber said Hollywood's dwindling pool of traditional mega-mergers is redirecting dealmaking toward creator businesses, individual IP, and independent production companies that can be built into larger businesses. Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): Any client with a large, owned audience and no business infrastructure around it is now a reachable acquisition target for the same capital that used to chase studio mergers, which argues for building the company (consumer products, live events, commercial partnerships) before a buyer prices the audience alone.
The Facts
  • Panelists: Raine Group partner Erik Hodge (leads Raine's entertainment/content practice), Loeb & Loeb partner John Kulback, Gerber Kawasaki CEO Ross Gerber, moderated by TheWrap's Roger Cheng, panel titled "The M&A Gold Rush in Media: Who's Next?"
  • Hodge: "There's a lot of opportunity around the migration of traditional talent, traditional content, onto YouTube." He cited Raine's investment in Moonbug Entertainment ("Cocomelon," "Blippi"), which assembled individual pieces of children's IP into consumer products, licensing and streaming before its sale to Candle Media, as the template.
  • Hodge pointed to Raine's investment in Uncensored, the digital network behind "Piers Morgan Uncensored": "With Piers, there's almost no difference between the show that he has on YouTube and the show that he used to have on Fox or CNN." Morgan's program can also be licensed as traditional TV programming.
  • Kulback said creator businesses that start with one personality and brand deals eventually need more sophisticated infrastructure: commercial executives who can secure larger partnerships, plus consumer-products and live-events expertise.
  • Gerber cited MrBeast as the model of an individual YouTube creator scaling into a broader content and consumer-products business, and said "there are many creators that have huge engagement that still have not even built out real businesses," a potential consolidation opportunity to combine creator-led companies into a more cohesive one.
  • Gerber separately cited his investment in Take-Two Interactive, framing gaming as another area of investor attention as entertainment moves across games, film and TV.
  • Hodge pointed to Mediawan's acquisition of Peter Chernin's North Road Company as M&A driven by access to resources and scale, not cost-cutting.
  • Kulback, who represented Google DeepMind in its research partnership and investment in A24, said emerging AI creator tools are blurring the line between technology IP and content IP, raising copyright, likeness and guild questions.
  • Gerber: "This is the best, most entrepreneurial time that I've ever seen" for creators, citing the combination of YouTube, AI and accessible production tools lowering the barriers to entering Hollywood.

Apple Studios Visual Effects Workers Win Their First IATSE Contract
Apple Studios visual effects workers ratified their first IATSE contract, securing minimum rates, AI protections from the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, employer-paid health and retirement benefits, and overtime and rest protections matching editorial crews.
IATSE announced Apple Studios VFX workers secured their first union contract, following the same path as VFX workers on "Avatar" and at Marvel and Disney, who ratified their first contracts last year. The agreement sets minimum rates per covered title tied to annual increases matching the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, minimum-hour guarantees, pay for all hours worked, overtime including holidays and sixth/seventh workdays, employer-paid Motion Picture Industry health care and pension benefits plus a defined-contribution retirement plan (effective retroactively to all hours worked since January 1), AI protections from the Basic Agreement, turnaround and rest protections matching editorial crews, meal penalties, and hazard pay for dangerous on-set conditions. IATSE International President Matthew D. Loeb said VFX workers have long powered major productions "without the union protections afforded to many of their colleagues."
Potential Talent Implication: A second major platform's VFX workforce organizing in successive years, each contract carrying explicit AI guardrails from the Basic Agreement, establishes AI-use protections as a now-standard term below-the-line crews expect on any production regardless of which studio or platform is financing it.
The Facts
  • Apple Studios visual effects workers secured their first IATSE contract, per IATSE's September 30 announcement.
  • Contract establishes minimum rates for every covered title; annual minimum-rate increases match those negotiated in the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement.
  • Workers secured minimum-hour guarantees, pay for all hours worked, and overtime protections including holidays and sixth/seventh workdays.
  • Employer-paid Motion Picture Industry health care, pension benefits, and a defined-contribution retirement savings plan; employer contributions to health/retirement plans apply retroactively to all hours worked since January 1, 2026.
  • Contract incorporates AI protections from the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, plus daily/weekly turnaround and rest protections matching editorial crews, meal penalties for violated lunch breaks, and additional pay for hazardous on-set conditions.
  • IATSE International President Matthew D. Loeb: "For too long, visual effects workers have powered some the industry's biggest productions without the union protections afforded to many of their colleagues. It is long past time to fix that."
  • Last year, VFX workers on "Avatar" and those working at Marvel and Disney ratified their first labor contracts, including overtime pay, Motion Picture Industry Pension and Health Plan eligibility, meal penalties, rest periods and turnaround times; the Disney/Marvel contract included 4% and 3.5% raises in its first two years, matching IATSE-negotiated raises.
